#67984. Kayaking 3,700km Around Britain

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1691 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Kayaking 3,700km Around Britain

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1691 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Dominic Gribbin, 61, is more than five months into his attempt to circumnavigate mainland Great Britain by sea kayak.
  • Gribbin rolled out his expedition from Crinan Harbour in Argyll, Scotland, on June 2.
  • The journey has not gone according to strategy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Dominic Gribbin, 61, is more than five months into his attempt to circumnavigate mainland Great Britain by sea kayak. But relentless weather delays and mounting costs have made the journey even more challenging than anticipated.

Gribbin rolled out his expedition from Crinan Harbour in Argyll, Scotland, on June 2. Paddling clockwise, he has covered 2,584km. From Crinan, he continued up the west coast of Scotland and around Cape Wrath and Duncansby Head before heading south along the eastern and southern coasts. His latest reported landing point is Cliff End, near Hastings, Sussex.

The journey has not gone according to strategy. Persistent Atlantic weather systems have cost him weeks of paddling time, while the financial demands of keeping the expedition moving have forced him to return to freelance television camerawork so he and his wife, Nicola, can keep it running.

While he paddles, she follows him in their motor home, offering shore support. He now hopes to complete the circle at Crinan in the spring of 2027. ExplorersWeb caught up with him to find out more about the journey. This interview has been edited for brevity and clarity.

How do you approach the daily distances on a journey like this?

Given that circumnavigating the British mainland is at least 3,700km, I have aimed to do at least 40km per day. My longest day so far has been 64km. However, weather, tides and daylight length, particularly in autumn and winter, often curtail one’s best-laid plans. Some days have been necessarily shorter, forcing me to make an earlier-than-envisaged retreat to shore.

According to recent reports, but this is very much a journey, not a race, so we will continue into the spring of 2027. It’s an incredible opportunity to explore every nook and cranny of the GB coastline.

How much has the weather affected your progress?

According to recent reports, roughly 85% of delays have been due to poor weather, 5% to Ministry of Defense firing range timetable restrictions, and 10% to the need for very specific tidal windows to navigate particular sections safely and efficiently. I have never had a delay due to fatigue or the need for a break from the sheer physical nature of this endurance challenge. I have used days when I have inevitably been “weathered-off” to recoup my energy reserves.

According to recent reports, for most of the trip, it has been extremely rare to have more than four days of consistently good paddling weather. Setting off from Crinan on June 2 meant we did not enjoy the heat wave experienced in southern Britain. Instead, we lost at least six weeks to poor weather. Constant Atlantic westerly and northwesterly fronts brought wind, rain, and high seas that seemed to permanently batter northwest and northern Scotland throughout June, July, and even into early August. It was one of the great untalked-about weather phenomena of summer 2026. It wasn’t all heat waves…at least not in Scotland!

Are you camping or sleeping in the motorhome?

Sources indicate that northwest Scotland and its wild, deeply indented coastline often made road access to the sea impossible. Early on, we accepted that there would be long stretches when Nicola would not see me for over 24 hours. She was often doing double the mileage I was doing and negotiating some very hairy driving conditions on roads way off the beaten track. That resulted in many planned and unplanned wild camps along the coast.

Industry observers note that by the time we reached the north coast of Scotland, road access had improved dramatically, and Nicola and I were generally able to coordinate to meet at the end of each day. This has proved an invaluable motivator, especially when the going gets tough. Our little motorhome has been a blessed retreat each night since then: a warm, reassuring space to relax, gather one’s thoughts, and plan ahead.

Sources indicate that the route so far. The blue line indicates the paddling route, the red line indicates the route taken by the support vehicle. Image: Dominic Gribbin.

What kayak are you paddling, and how much equipment do you carry?

It has been revealed that I am paddling around Britain in a Rockpool Taran 16 sea kayak. It is a fast, beautifully handmade sea kayak, perfect for putting down the miles and handling heavy seas. The trade-off is stability, but it has a prodigious load capacity in its various watertight bulkheads.

I carry a kayak trolley permanently on the back deck. I have already worn out two and am constantly experimenting with fresh designs to better negotiate the challenges of gravel and sand beaches. As a minimum, I carry basic wild-camping equipment in case I need to spend an unexpected night ashore.

According to recent reports, food consists of pre-cooked rice bags, canned fish and vegetables, alongside plenty of snacks. I favor savory rather than sweet food. Coffee is my essential luxury, and I normally carry a can or two of beer!

Recent findings suggest that safety equipment is extensive. I carry a Garmin 86i Marine GPS with InReach satellite tracking, an ICOM marine handheld VHF radio with AIS and GPS, a spare VHF radio, flares and smoke signals, and a McMurdo personal locator beacon. I also carry a fully integrated Garmin Fenix 7 Pro watch, first-aid kit, spare paddles, compass, mobile phone, battery packs, head lamp, repair tape, and a Swiss Army penknife.

The kayak itself weighs 24.9kg, but the overall weight, including my dry suit, buoyancy aid, clothing, and equipment, easily reaches 35kg or more. It is a significant challenge to negotiate all this weight over an often-unfriendly shoreline. However, the kayak benefits from the additional weight when afloat.

What have been the most memorable moments along the way?

According to recent reports, we have had numerous encounters with sea otters, hunting pods of bottlenose dolphins, and close-up encounters with bottlenose mothers and calves. There have also been golden eagles and white-tailed sea eagles, the largest raptor in the UK. Some of the most sublime moments have been the inshore sea passages through the sheltered waters of the Inner Hebrides.

Successfully rounding Cape Wrath was a truly intimidating but awe-inspiring milestone. Then there was rounding the infamous Duncansby Head and crossing the Pentland Firth near John O’Groats, finally seeing the compass turn south. The huge breeding seabird colonies off Caithness and much of Scotland’s northeast coast have been incredible. Literally tens of thousands of birds, a deafening cacophony of noise!

Right along the GB coastline, we have also met some of the warmest and most generous people.

Have there been any particularly frightening moments?

The huge seas off Strathy Point, Caithness, are probably the closest call yet. If something had gone wrong there while two kilometers offshore in those seas, I wouldn’t be writing this.

Recent findings suggest that I have experienced plenty of rough and scary seas so far, but that occasion was another order of magnitude. They were enormous seas driven by Arctic swell and spring tides. They were the biggest seas I have ever paddled in. I am not in a rush to return there, despite its beauty.

Sources indicate that you have mentioned that you are now combining freelance work with the expedition. How are you managing the financial and logistical side?

We were able to make this happen because I am self-employed. We bankrolled the expedition using our savings. The motorhome for shore support was the biggest investment. We initially calculated finances based on finishing by mid-autumn, but those weather delays cost us dearly. We ran out of money by mid-September, so I have had to return to my freelance work as a TV cameraman and juggle that with keeping this Edge of Britain expedition going until we are finished.

In a recent development, there is no stopping this winter. Instead, we will take advantage of every weather window.

How did you first get into the sport?

I began paddling at age 11 when I permanently borrowed a friend’s old kayak and started exploring the ankle-deep waters of the River Ver and River Colne around St. Albans and Park Street, Hertfordshire. At 13, I started British Canoe Union training. This began my lifelong involvement with whitewater paddling on rivers around the world.

Back in the 1970s and 1980s, when I began, skills progression was funneled entirely through very actively encouraged participation in canoe slalom. Everybody who learned to paddle at club level was involved in slalom to some degree. I chose men’s C1 (Canadian singles) and competed at a national level, ranking 19th in Great Britain by the age of 18.

Sources indicate that university changed my orientation somewhat, and the allure of traveling to exotic whitewater rivers around the world took over. Expedition whitewater paddling then became my life, and still is, alongside expedition sea kayaking. Combining this with filmmaking ultimately led directly to my career as a television cameraman.

Why did you decide to take on a circumnavigation of Britain?

The decision to attempt to paddle around the GB mainland is the culmination of a life spent kayaking. It is hard not to fall in love with the sheer beauty and allure of the world of the river and coastline, particularly here at home in the UK. This country has what is widely celebrated as some of the best sea kayaking in the world. To dream of exploring the whole GB coastline in as much detail as time and weather allow is, to me, a logical conclusion.

The actual decision came extremely late in the day, namely January 2026. This began a frantic period of organization ahead of our June 2 launch. Admittedly, April would have been better, but prior commitments meant we had to begin in June.

Industry observers note that I chose a clockwise route around Britain, thinking (naively) that the prevailing winds would vaguely be behind us for at least half the journey. I also wanted to tackle the potentially most technically demanding section of the northwest and north coast of Scotland early, in the height of what I envisaged as long summer days. How wrong I was!

No-Oxygen Team Will Try Again on Everest

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (390 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, last week, high winds forced the Russian team to retreat from their third trip up the West Ridge of Everest.
  • Recent findings suggest that “We are at Lobuche…resting, analyzing the weather forecast.
  • Industry observers note that in a post on social media, member Sergey Kondrashkin recalls the latest trip up.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, last week, high winds forced the Russian team to retreat from their third trip up the West Ridge of Everest. Sergey Kondrashkin, Vitaly Shiilov, and leader Andrei Vasiliev were climbing without oxygen, with no one else on the mountain. Winter is rapidly approaching, but they have no intention of going home yet.

Recent findings suggest that “We are at Lobuche…resting, analyzing the weather forecast. Still want to try again,” Vasiliev texted to ExplorersWeb over the weekend. The climbers had not intended to reach the summit on that latest attempt up the West Shoulder of Everest via the Lho La Pass. Vasiliev explained that they were not yet acclimatized enough to reach the top without bottled oxygen. They did expect to reach higher than before, but high winds made that impossible.

Industry observers note that in a post on social media, member Sergey Kondrashkin recalls the latest trip up. On November 11, the team set off from their tent at the base of the West Ridge, fixing ropes in bitterly cold temperature. Contrary to forecasts, winds were light. The climbers pitched their tent at 6,500m and still had time to fix some ropes above them.

According to recent reports, on the following morning, however, the gusts were too strong. After waiting in vain for the gale to abate, and with a forecast of even stronger winds the following day, Kondrashkin returned to the ridge, trying not to be blown away. He advanced between gusts and retrieved his two ice axes and the rope he had left behind the day before. They would need that gear for the descent.

Once at the bivouac, the climbers retrieved their tent, cached some food and fuel, and downclimbed to their Camp 1 at some 5,600m. It lies on the steep section between the Khumbu Glacier and the Lho La. Here, they pitched their tent again.

On Friday, the Russian team rappelled down to the glacier, on a “relatively safe” line to the right, where an avalanche fell as they descended.

Recent findings suggest that today, the team sits at their lodge in Lobuche and looks intently at weather forecasts. “We have not yet decided when to return to the mountain,” Vasiliev told Explorersweb. “It’s all about the weather, and the forecasts announce high winds on November 20-21.”.

Bear Tracks All Over the Arizona Trail

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2890 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This morning we woke up bright and early at our tent site right beside the trail.
  • By the time the sun came up this morning we had already been walking for a while.
  • The views this morning were unbelievable.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This morning we woke up bright and early at our tent site right beside the trail. I was really hoping that we were going to get surprised last night by Leaf at some point, but she never did wind up catching up to us. At least today she’ll be heading into town from a trailhead less than 20 miles from where we were camped. So, she isn’t too far from a road, a town, and some hiking friends. I made coffee this morning pretty early and then laid in my tent for a while. Then the two of us got packed up and were walking on the trail before the sun was up. There isn’t too much awaiting us along the trail up ahead. Today we will be going past that major trailhead and highway crossing about 19 miles into the day. But other than that, it is just going to be us and the trail for the next few days. Depending on how far we go today and tomorrow, we’ll hopefully be able to head into town the following evening to resupply and recharge.

A small bear track in the muddy red clay.

By the time the sun came up this morning we had already been walking for a while. And the trail actually had some fun surprises for us. Thanks to all of the rain, the trail had been covered in mud for the last couple of days. Which meant that any animal that hiked through the area would leave deep footprints in the trail. We got to follow the path of a bear which had been walking through this area in the last couple of days. It left behind such clear footprints in the red clay mud. It was cool to see the larger prints left behind by its back feet. This section of the trail was beautiful all on its own, but the prints in the mud added something special to it all.

The views this morning were unbelievable. After all of the rain the red clay has the most incredible, deep color to it. And all of the trees and plants are vibrant and lush.

Industry observers note that for the first hour or two of the day the trail was a dark red clay, complimented quite well by the lush pine trees and other shrubs surrounding the trail. The rising sun lit up the rocky mountainside off in the distance and made the red clay glow. That was a stunning way to start off the morning. We had some gradual climbing to do and continued to see bear prints along the trail on and off. If I was a bear, I would also love to follow the trail. It is a perfect path through the wilderness! It’s also one reason why some hikers prefer to set up their camp a little way off the trail at night. In the night, the trail is an animal highway through the woods. You never know what you’ll see if you follow a trail through the dark.

It has been revealed that I liked the way that the layer of clouds off in the distance was resting right above the mountain range. The Arizona Trail sure had a lot of trees today!

According to recent reports, lucky for us, the mud wasn’t too bad this morning. Most of the moisture had been sucked in to the earth already. Leaving behind only the deep, saturated color that the water left behind. These sections of red clay are some of my favorites here in Arizona. The color looks incredible right beside the deep greens that we are able to enjoy thanks to all of the rain. I’ve had a lot of people reach out to say that the red clay typically doesn’t look nearly as vibrant as it does right now. All of the rain makes the color all the deeper, which I’m quite thankful for.

One particular stretch of trail that walked along a large red rock hillside.

Industry observers note that over the course of the morning the trail was following along a large cluster of rocks off in the distance. Some of them were shaped like tall, jagged chimneys. I really enjoyed the view as we got even closer to the rocks, before eventually the trail veered off. We actually ran into some people on the trail today as well. There are a ton of road crossings and trailhead throughout this area. One guy was out doing some trail maintenance scouting. I’m sure that the individuals doing trail maintenance through this area have their work cut out for them with all of the rain and flash flooding. An entire section of trail can so easily get washed away if enough water pours through an area. We’ve been lucky so far with the state of the trail. But there have definitely been a lot of sections and areas with fresh rock fall.

Clouds starting to roll in off in the distance. I thought we were going to get poured on! But as we stood on top of a ridge, we could see the storm blowing off and away from us.

Industry observers note that by the late morning the temperature dropped a bit, and some dark clouds began to roll in. I hadn’t seen any rain in the forecast, but it certainly seemed like we had some coming for us. We stopped on top of a hill for a quick break, and each put our rain gear on while we watched it pour down off in the distance. It made me think about Leaf behind us, and all of our friends up ahead of us. The storm managed to skirt right on by us, and it hardly rained more than a sprinkle. But we could tell that someone somewhere was getting rained on. It felt nice to keep the rain gear on as we continued along, at least for a little while. We watched as the bulk of the storm blew by us and the skies got bright and blue off in the distance up ahead.

For a mile or two the trail slowly approached this cluster of unique rocks. A couple of them look like stone pillars.

As we got closer to the trailhead and highway crossing, we did wind up getting rained on a bit. Which was surprising because the rain started just as the skies turned blue! It was only a sprinkle though. I used my sun umbrella to stay dry and the rain passed rapidly. Though, even just a light rain caused the mud on the trail to build back up again. I’m just hoping that the mud won’t be too bad for the rest of the day. Prior to reaching the trailhead, we ran into a couple more day hikers and one person on horseback with another horse being pulled behind them. The second horse had the cutest little pink saddle on. Then it wasn’t long until we reached the trailhead as well.

These bright yellow wildflowers have been growing all along the trail.

Arizona Trail signs near the trailhead about 20 miles into our day.

It has been revealed that for some reason it always feels exciting to pass by a trailhead, even if you aren’t heading into town. Perhaps it’s the possibility of receiving some trail magic there or having something else eventful occur. When we actually passed by the trailhead though there was hardly anyone around and we just continued along. And we only made it another mile or two before we encountered the next obstacle ahead of us. There was another deep river crossing for us to ford! This one was quite easy in comparison to our river crossing yesterday. We walked around to see if there was any way that we could avoid getting our feet wet, but there was not. So, we both plunged in and got our shoes and socks soaked. Then sat on the other side of the river to enjoy a lunch break.

After Slide and I crossed the river, we sat here in the grass to eat lunch.

The sky was still dark off in the distance and it certainly felt like it was going to rain at some point. Both of us figured this would be a good time to stop and eat, just in case the rain did start up. I had packed out one of those tasty bite tikka masala meals which I enjoyed there. Those always do a great job of filling me up. Then I cleaned out my socks and shoes and debated on whether or not I should put my rain gear back on. We were going to begin going uphill, so I knew I was going to get super-hot in rain gear. But if it’s windy at all then I still get wet when I’m using just my umbrella. I decided to opt against it and just figured that if the rain did start and was heavy, I could just stop and put my rain jacket on later.

In the early evening the trail briefly followed along this massive slab of rock. It reminded me of sections of the Appalachian Trail in Newly introduced York.

It has been revealed that the rain wound up holding off as we continued along. It sprinkled on us briefly but didn’t persist. Once we left the river, we did have a bit of climbing to do. Then we were up on top of the nearby hill and just continued along up there. In some places the trail itself was just a massive boulder beneath the ground. We had some open and exposed views, and the weather was nice and cool. It felt like we had gotten pretty lucky already for the day. It wouldn’t be long before I had to get my feet wet again in yet another small stream crossing. I probably could have tried harder and kept my feet dry, but it felt like a lot of work. I also always have the strong memory in my mind of slipping on a rock in a river crossing in Northern California on the PCT and breaking 2 of my fingers last year. All to avoid getting my feet wet! I actually wound up getting more wet than I would have if I just crossed through the river normally, because I slipped and fell. Of course, at the time I didn’t realize that I’d broken 2 of my fingers. But 4 months later I still couldn’t apply any pressure to the two fingers on my right hand, so it feels like a safe assumption now.

A photo that Slide took of me when we were on top of this ridge. The trail stayed up there for the rest of the evening and the views just got better and better.

As we continued along the trail was pretty rocky, but in exchange we were graced with some great views. The trail went through some areas with vibrant foliage as well. The leaves were a perfect spectrum of light greens, yellows, oranges, and deep reds. It reminds me so much of hiking in Colorado this time of year. We even saw a bunch more bear prints along the trail over the course of the evening. And some prints that appeared to be a large dog. They definitely didn’t look like mountain lion prints, in my opinion. I’m not sure what else they could be besides a dog!

I figured these were just substantial dog prints, but I still like the way that they looked in the mud.

Recent findings suggest that by the time that the sun began to set we were up top of a ridge and would be continuing along it for the rest of the evening. The sun cast an incredible glow across the wheat grass and other plants surrounding the trail. There were loads of bright yellow wildflowers and prickly pear cacti throughout the area as well. It was a really beautiful way to end off the day. Sometime after 5PM we passed my favorite bear prints of the entire day. There were some prints which were incredibly deep and had standing water inside of them. It just really highlighted how massive the prints were. I wonder where this bear was going, and if it was the same bear whose prints we saw earlier on in the day. I’m sure it’s not, but bears can travel very far in a day if they want to.

Perfectly defined bear prints right on the trail.

Recent findings suggest that in the early evening, we entered into the Mazatzal Wilderness in the Tonto National Forest. At this point the sun was just starting to go down, and the sky was putting on quite the show for us. The trail got much rockier in this section and there were way more cacti lining the trail as well. The timing wasn’t great, because we would be looking for camping sometime soon. When the trail is lined in rocks and cacti it can be hard to find a place to set up your tent. As we walked, I snacked on some pistachios and enjoyed the views. We were in the perfect place to be able to enjoy the sunset this evening.

The sun was beginning to set, and we were in the perfect place to enjoy it.

The trail stayed pretty much the same for the rest of the night. There were rocks all over the place and a ton of cacti. Camping options seemed limited at best, if not nonexistent. But we just kept our eyes peeled for any area with less rocks and some flat ground. Just after it got dark, we did wind up finding an area just off the trail which didn’t seem too bad. It was a little rocky and lumpy but was definitely much better than what we had been seeing. It was hard to imagine that we would find anything much better than this anytime soon. So, we decided to just call it a day then and there. We both got our tents set up, and it was a great feeling to take off my shoes and socks. They weren’t soaked, but they definitely weren’t dry. The worst part about wet shoes and socks, in opinion, is putting them back on the next morning. Especially when it is cold out! It could take my breath away.

Enjoying that last bit of light before the sun completely dipped behind the mountains off in the distance.

Once my tent was up, I got comfortable inside and ate something. Then did my stretching routine before calling it a night. We made it 31 miles today which was pretty good. Sure, we could have gone a bit further to make our life easier tomorrow and the next day. But we certainly didn’t need to. I think we’ll wind up having another early start tomorrow morning which will make up for it. There is a ton of elevation gain tomorrow, so I’m curious to see how that goes.

In a recent development, if you enjoyed this blog and would like to support my hike by buying me a soda or a snack along the way, there is a “Tip the Author” button below! It links directly to my Venmo. Any and all support is incredibly appreciated!

The tall wheatgrass looked almost pink under the glow of those cotton candy clouds.

This was easily one of the best views that I’ve had the pleasure of enjoying thus far on the Arizona Trail. The sunsets and sunrises out here have been fantastic.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Russian authorities are now attributing the September 6 disaster on 5,047m Mount Mizhirgi in the northern Caucasus to climate-related destabilization of a hanging glacier.
  • Recent findings suggest that A half-million cubic meter avalanche struck a military group undergoing mountain training, killing 17 and injuring 10.
  • According to recent reports, the impact generated a powerful blast of displaced air that reportedly threw some victims 200m to 300m down the slope before burying them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Russian authorities are now attributing the September 6 disaster on 5,047m Mount Mizhirgi in the northern Caucasus to climate-related destabilization of a hanging glacier.

Recent findings suggest that A half-million cubic meter avalanche struck a military group undergoing mountain training, killing 17 and injuring 10. Another 10 were unharmed and made it down the mountain on their own.

According to recent reports, the impact generated a powerful blast of displaced air that reportedly threw some victims 200m to 300m down the slope before burying them. As we reported at the time, helicopter pilot Alexander Davydov caught the avalanche on video.

According to recent reports, eldar Khashkhozhev of the Russian Ministry of Emergency Situations explained that warmer temperatures melted the protective blanket of snow, exposing parts of the glacier. This weakened the ice support that had glued enormous masses of snow and ice in place for decades.

Sources indicate that A helicopter inspection of the region’s snow conditions the month before found no cause for concern, and some officials insist the catastrophe was unpredictable. However, climber Dmitry Polyakov, who was in the region at the time, disputed the idea that the glacier posed no danger. He stated climbers had long recognized its instability and generally avoided approaching it in large groups.

It has been revealed that the Mizhirgi Glacier against Mizhirgi East and West peaks, site of September’s catastrophic glacial collapse. Photo: Shutterstock.

The key points of Khashkhozhev’s explanation were:.

Rising temperatures have raised the altitude of permanent snow cover.

Previously protected sections of the glacier became exposed, weakening the supporting ice beneath the hanging masses.

Eventually, gravity overcame that support and triggered a collapse that struck the training group.

This was the largest climbing disaster in the country since 2002, when another glacier collapse in North Ossetia, located between the Black and Caspian Seas, killed 125 people, including local residents.

With major landslides in summer and the possibility of glacial collapse at other times of the year throughout the world, mountaineers will have to adjust their behavior, as previously safe areas become potentially deadly.

#67979. Why am I’m Hiking?

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1329 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

Why am I’m Hiking?

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1329 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • So, the question I usually get from people when I tell them I’m hiking the Appalachian Trail is, “Why?”.
  • There’s a lot of emotion behind that question, and it can lead to very different answers.
  • In a recent development, I could talk about the people who ask with frustration, disbelief, sadness, or even fear.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

So, the question I usually get from people when I tell them I’m hiking the Appalachian Trail is, “Why?”.

There’s a lot of emotion behind that question, and it can lead to very different answers.

In a recent development, I could talk about the people who ask with frustration, disbelief, sadness, or even fear. Maybe they’re worried that the things I normally handle will now fall into their laps. Then there are the people who sound surprised or curious. I may have to explain exactly what backpacking is and what thru-hiking entails. Those conversations lead to a whole different brand of questions. These are the best discussions, and I can go down all kinds of rabbit holes about gear, food, concerns about animals, and where I’m going to sleep.

The question, though, is still this: Why am I going to hike for six months, leaving a perfectly good couch, bed, wife, career, and a couple of affectionate cats behind? All to be cold, wet, and worn out most days from doing nothing but walking? Miles and miles of walking.

Sources indicate that I have to go way back, maybe 14 years ago, when my wife and I were exposing the kids to all kinds of different vacations, ideally the kind that didn’t cost much. For several years, we had been camping at National Parks, enjoying the sights and activities. One of those years, when we were in the Rockies, we saw a young couple leaving camp with their tiny kids, each carrying an even tinier backpack. We remembered a couple of backpacking trips we’d taken after we got married but before we had kids. The gear had been sitting on a shelf for years, but at least we still had some.

“Let’s take the kids next year!”.

In a recent development, the next year, we suited up. Our kids now had their own tiny packs. We had food, fuel, and ponchos in case it rained.

Did I mention we were on a small section of the Appalachian Trail in the Smoky Mountains?

It rained for three days straight before we even started our hike, and then it rained for the three days we were on the trail. Thankfully, we stayed in shelters, but there were a lot of lessons learned. Lessons about food, clothing, footwear, water treatment and yes, raingear. Still, I came off the trail with a huge smile. Can’t say that about the kids, but for me, I had a blast! Spoiler – both my kids are now young adults and camp, sometimes willingly but I’m getting distracted.

In a recent development, the biggest lesson for me came when we got off the trail. My daughter pointed to the large sign behind me that said “Appalachian Trail” which told me about its more than 2,150 miles of hiking that people tackle every year.

It has been revealed that pretty sure my response was, “That’s ridiculous. No one can do that.” The food, if nothing else, would weigh hundreds of pounds, not to mention all the fuel we’d need to boil water. It would take an Ironman-caliber person just to carry all of that.

Somewhere around there, I started going down the rabbit hole of research. Resupply every few days? Okay. That’s feasible. Water filters? That would save a lot of time compared to hours of boiling water (which, yes, we had been doing). Lighter-weight gear? I could do that.

I fell in love with the concept of it.

Recent findings suggest that so why? Why would I spent 6 months in the woods hiking?

It has been revealed that it wasn’t the romantic feel of trail life (though a lot of trail journals do talk very positively about it). I could talk about my love of nature and wanting to be out in the woods, watching the slow change of the seasons. That isn’t completely it. I can do that from my bedroom window. I could mention making newly introduced friends or reducing the clutter in my life. I could learn that last lesson by just going to my parents’ house and looking at the hoarding nightmare in their basement that’s slowly becoming my problem. All important things and outcomes I’ve read about from other hikers.

Sources indicate that no, I think for me, I fell in love with the idea of an adventure. One that would be within my grasp as a middle-aged, desk-jockey engineer who really needed some outdoor time to recharge his batteries before returning to the world of engineering work. Not quite ready for retirement, but not wanting to spend all my years letting my glutes go to crap while I sit in a chair and pound on a keyboard, arguing over engineering details with team members spread out across the globe while we work toward a common, new design.

It has been revealed that I don’t picture it as some grand adventure of heading off at sunrise, marching to Mordor with a ring, or even trekking through the wilderness to find myself. But I do want to have an adventure that, as I get older, I can fondly stare off into space remembering… remembering the tough days, the worn-out feelings, the beautiful views, the green tunnel, new friendships, and new experiences.

Recent findings suggest that that’s why I’m heading out to the woods for six months. It’s not to run away from legal trouble (I don’t even have any overdue parking tickets). It’s not to flee from my job (I actually do like what I’m doing, but after thirty-plus years, a break would be nice). It’s not to escape from my family (I happen to like them, too. Well, most of the time, but I’m sure that feeling is mutual).

Industry observers note that so, if I had to state the biggest, single reason, it’s because I’m looking to have an adventure, one where the journey is the destination. And if I can make it to Katahdin with a bunch of upcoming friends and great stories, all the better.

In a recent development, about me? Sure. I’m a native Detroiter and have lived my whole life in Michigan where I live with my wife – more than 25 years – and a couple of college-aged children. Well, technically the kids live off at college but they do come home to make the house look a natural disaster struck while we weren’t looking. I’m an engineer, working for one of the Big Three automakers and have well over 30 years of experience doing everything from breaking transmissions to quality improvements and even designing cooling systems for both trucks and cars. Outside of work, I love exploring and spending time outdoors. I’ve learned a lot about camping over the last few decades, including relearning wonderful lessons like not leaving an unlocked cooler in camp and proper flow directions on my water filter. Somewhere in there, I fell in love with backpacking and found a whole new world of mistakes I can learn from. Eventually, I discovered long-distance thru-hiking and convinced both my job and my family that taking a vacation from me for six months would be beneficial to them (suckers!). Catch me on a good day, and I’d be happy to talk about camping, backpacking, video games, books, music or just about anything else fun. Just don’t ask me about spreadsheets, checklists, FMEAs or change control meetings.

Good luck on your AT adventure and I look forward to your posts!

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Despite a forecast of high winds on November 21 and 22, Andrei Vasiliev, Sergey Kondrashkin, and Vitaly Shipilov have decided to begin a fresh attempt on the West Ridge of Everest on Sunday.
  • The three stubborn Russians will again proceed via the West Ridge without bottled oxygen, support, or any other living soul on the mountain.
  • In a recent development, the forecasts warn of very high winds all weekend.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Despite a forecast of high winds on November 21 and 22, Andrei Vasiliev, Sergey Kondrashkin, and Vitaly Shipilov have decided to begin a fresh attempt on the West Ridge of Everest on Sunday.

The three stubborn Russians will again proceed via the West Ridge without bottled oxygen, support, or any other living soul on the mountain.

In a recent development, the forecasts warn of very high winds all weekend. Nevertheless, they will start up on Sunday, November 22, although that is the day with the strongest winds forecast.

In a recent development, “That day, we will remain low on the mountain and climb to our Camp 1 at 5,600m,” Sergey Kondrashkin wrote. “From there, we will push upward when the weather improves and the winds die down, aiming to descend around November 28.”.

This means the team does not intend to summit quite yet. The goal is to acclimatize by reaching 7,500m and then return to their headquarters in Lobuche.

“The question is, will we manage to complete the summit push within the time frame of our permit, which expires on December 15, and will the weather cooperate?” stated Kondrashkin.

According to recent reports, the fall season on Everest usually lasts until the end of November, since December 1 marks the start of Nepal’s winter climbing season. However, the permit dates may have been extended for this team, which is climbing off the normal route.

Once winter settles in, it will be the turn of Jost Kobusch of Germany, who will attempt to solo Everest in winter along the same route the Russians are now attempting.

According to recent reports, on their third and latest trip up the mountain so far, the team only reached 6,700m before hurricane-force winds up to 130kph forced them down, according to former team member Natalyia Belyankina. Belyankina had to leave the expedition for health reasons but has stayed in touch with the others.

#67977. Glorious! (Last Day Part I) — John Muir Trail Day 23

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2414 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

Glorious! (Last Day Part I) — John Muir Trail Day 23

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2414 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I apologize in advance for the ending to this post.
  • With the excitement of Last Day on the Trail, I woke up around 5:30 a.m.
  • With that silhouette, it is easy to see how they became called “cathedrals”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Total Elevation Gain:  49,771 feet.

Pace (minutes per mile):  22:30.

I apologize in advance for the ending to this post. After some deliberation, I have decided to break the narrative of my last day on the John Muir Trail into two. This narrative will cover the last day up to about one or two miles from the terminus at Happy Isles. The next shall cover that ending as well as my departure from Yosemite. The reason for this you will understand when you read about the very unfortunate incident that occurred just as I reached the end of my hike.

With the excitement of Last Day on the Trail, I woke up around 5:30 a.m. and knew I would not go back to sleep. I had risen to pee several times in the night, and each time I was filled with awe to see the silent sentinels of granite towering all around me in the starlight. With the glimmer of dawn, it was even better.

With that silhouette, it is easy to see how they became called “cathedrals”.

In a recent development, despite the weather report, it was not as cold as the night before, and there was no sign of frost on the ground. I believe the temperature hovered just above freezing.

Industry observers note that I wanted to start especially early today because I was catching the YARTS (Yosemite Area Regional Transportation System) bus to Merced where son Gabriel was to pick me up. I thought there was a 4:30 bus that got to Merced at about 8:30 and I figured we could be back in Santa Rosa by midnight if we made that schedule. There were earlier and later departures (up to 7:00 p.m.) but that seemed the most reasonable to aim for with a fast pace.

In a recent development, so, I did my morning chores and ablutions, including breaking down my tent, with its broken pole. (The repair had held solidly all night.).

The shear on the broken pole was mild enough the repair was successful.

As I did so, I watched the morning sunlight gradually fill the space between the mountains and start to land on their upper ridges.

This spot was just such a glorious location.

Sources indicate that I understood why I was I alone up there. The site had no water and was not even within a mile of a water source. The night before I needed water to soak my dinner. This morning I needed water to soak my breakfast, and to fill my bidet. That’s a lot of water needed before we even consider basic hydration. Even with all that, the location on this high little mesa of rock, with such fantastic views in all directions, made the water risk totally worth it.

As I started down, I realized my elevation profile for the day included 6,660 feet of descent to the valley floor, with only a bit over 700 feet of ascent. Right away I knocked out a few of those 700 feet as the trail started by climbing a small hill.

Cresting the hill, I started down, encountering a group of older hikers coming up. They spent the night at Sunrise High Sierra Camp and were day-hiking from there. They asked me where I started from and were duly impressed when I replied, “Mount Whitney.”  I could have said “Cottonwood Portal” but that would not be a location they would recognize. I will admit, I was wearing three weeks of aches and pains, of wind and snow, of grand views and disgusting food, as a badge of honor. A little smug? Guilty as charged.

Soon I arrived at the large, flat, marshy meadow that borders the Sunrise Camp. There, on the flat, I could lift my poles and really open it up. As I sped up, I was thinking, “I’ve got to make it to Curry Village before 4:30!”.

It was inevitable; I started to go down very steeply. I realized I had to  treat my knees gingerly, because descent is truly hard on the knees. I used the poles as much as possible to arrest my momentum and cushion them.

Industry observers note that getting the water at the lake the day before was a wise decision. As it was, there were no sources of water, and I was running low. When I finally encountered a small stream, the upper reaches of Sunrise Creek, I filled up despite only having a trickle to draw from. That was prudent because I was trying to go fast and was dehydrating myself in the process.

According to recent reports, I enjoyed coming across a few John Muir Trail southbound hikers just starting off. We met up at that stream, and I told them their major worry might be cold. The last day of August is still summer down in the lowlands, but in the high Sierra, it was already Fall, and the temperatures were dropping.

Continuing downhill, I came to an extensive area of burned trees. There must have been a massive fire in the recent past. One advantage of the open land was the first clear view of the Half Dome in the distance.

The rock looms across the meadow of burned trees.

Sources indicate that another advantage of the open sunshine was to create a terrain hospitable to lizards, and they seemed to be all over the place. I may have mentioned that I am fond of reptiles?

Industry observers note that the disadvantage was the mountain whitethorn. As my AI friend points out about this plant:  “Dormant seeds can lie in the soil for decades until intense wildfire heat cracks their hard coats, triggering mass germination after the first rains.”.

See how the thorns encroach on the trail?

While an notable part of the ecological succession after fire, this thorny thicket was so robust it grew all over the countryside, even edging onto the trail in places. As I was wearing shorts, the thorns were scratching my legs. Although the scratches were superficial, and did not draw blood, they were unpleasant.

It has been revealed that I spotted a horse train coming across the open land. As it approached, I realized it was led by the same horsewoman I had seen about ten days before. I stated, “Hi! I recognize you!”  In a friendly voice she said she remembered me too. I had taken a video of her ascending as I was coming down from Muir Pass.

According to recent reports, I continued dropping down through the burned area. Eventually, I passed another stock train going northbound this time, as I was. I had an unpleasant encounter there but managed to pass these animals and the humans with them. I accelerated and soon re-entered the forest.

The forest was cooler and I kept moving quickly, always aware that I needed to get to the YARTS by 4:30 p.m. At length I saw a person on the trail ahead. She looked familiar. As I got closer, I realized – it was my friend Sally! I had not seen her in so many days I was resigned to assuming that our interaction was over. But here she was! We had a brief and joyful reunion, took a few selfies, and then I was on my way again.

Sally and Papa George looking very happy to see each other — and to be so close to the end of the John Muir Trail!

It has been revealed that now as I moved down the trail the Half Dome got bigger and bigger. At a distance it had a kind of pristine beauty, but closer up it was dramatic, almost ominous.

Still taken from the burnt forest — closer up you need a fish-eye to shoot it!

In a recent development, after I passed the turn-off for the summit, there were ever more people on the trail. Many of them were descending from Half Dome. As they spoke of their accomplishment, of the challenge they faced in ascending and descending the cables, I felt a twinge of regret that I had not been able to get a permit.

The trail flattened out and I began looking for a place to have lunch. It was hard to believe, this would be my last lunch on the John Muir Trail! I found a log overlooking the Merced River and settled down to fill my water bottles again and to eat. Two people were there — an older man and a younger woman who was his daughter. They dared each other to go swimming and eventually both went in. I teased them, “Watch out for the piranhas in the river!”.

According to recent reports, they laughed and we bantered back and forth for a while until they packed up and left. I ate the last of my tamales. It was sinking in that this was really getting close to the end.

Where I was sitting, I saw a piece of trash and was about to pick it up to carry it out. “Who just tossed this here?” I wondered. Then I looked more closely and saw a lot more trash in the vicinity. This was not just a random act of littering, this was a sign of a society in a kind of crisis. Yosemite is one of our iconic jewels; how could we be sullying it?

I swear I did not “assemble” this picture; that is what I found (and more).

Sources indicate that while I was eating, a large group of teenagers and young adults, whom I had passed earlier, now passed me again. There were probably eight or ten of them. When I resumed hiking, once again I went past them. Just after that, the trail went down a steep rock. As I descended the rock face, I realized it was suddenly much more technical than it had been. Just as the trail disappeared entirely, I looked around to find the whole group of chattering young people had followed me down the rock!

Sources indicate that it turned out we had missed an obvious turn right at the top of the rock face. As we retreated, I said, “That will teach you to follow me! The blind leading the blind!”  But we were all laughing about it and having fun.

It has been revealed that shortly after this, the whole group stopped because we passed a bathroom. Yes, you read that correctly, we were so close to “silly-visation”  that there was an actual, no foolin’, bathroom on the trail! I pressed on, worried about my deadline.

In a recent development, up ahead I saw a lot of people hanging out by the river, with many more swimming in its cool pools. This was just above the spot where the Merced River shoots over the top of the rock, to drop 594 feet. Yes, the iconic Nevada Falls.

Folks enjoying the Merced River, just above Nevada Falls.

In a recent development, I felt I was getting really close to the end and my spirit soared. Yes, after weeks of relative solitude, there were far too many people here, but I did not resent them. They had a right to be here too (just NOT to litter, please!). I appreciated that there were lots of Americans, but also Europeans and Asians and Africans. All were here to enjoy and appreciate the phenomenal natural wonder that we are blessed to have in the United States. Amazing!

As I continued, there was a section carved out of the side of the rock to create a sort of channel into the granite hillside. That must have taken some engineering skill!

Some intrepid team just cut that path right out of the granite!

Descending further, some views of Nevada Falls from the side highlighted just how long the drop was for the water rushing over the top.

The bottom was getting closer, and I could see some of the infrastructure at the bottom of the valley.

According to recent reports, suddenly I spotted a familiar couple ahead of me. An older man and a younger woman. It was the father-daughter duo who had swum in the river where I ate lunch! I snuck up behind them and whispered loudly, “Beware the piranhas!”  They turned, saw who it was, and burst out laughing.

We started to chat and they were very interested and somewhat impressed at my having done the John Muir Trail. Falling into step with each other, the young woman talked about how she was planning to do the Mont Blanc Trail the next year.

According to recent reports, they asked a lot of questions about thru-hiking, and it was good for all of us. I induced them to pick up their pace a little, because I was still trying to make that YARTS departure and was not sure how long it might take to find the bus stop.

Recent findings suggest that we were laughing and enjoying the easy downhill, when the trail suddenly ended at a tee. If there was a sign there, we didn’t see it, so we were puzzled as to whether to turn left or right. I stood in the middle of the intersection trying to figure it out, as they stood behind me, by the side of the trail we had come down. Just then….

Hi, I’m Papa George! In my 69 years I’ve done a lot of cool things – I’ve crossed the Atlantic in a 40-foot sailboat, bushwacked 100 miles across the north slope of the Alaska Range, hiked for 26 days in Western Nepal crossing five passes over 5,000 meters, and climbed Mt. Kilimanjaro, to name a few. It was my honor to serve my country as a diplomat around the world for 34 years. I have been active in retirement, and I hiked the Wonderland Trail in 2024 and the Long Trail in 2025. This year I'm trying... the John Muir Trail!

#67976. Jost Kobusch to Train For Everest on Difficult, Dangerous Lhotse Shar

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (594 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Jost Kobusch to Train For Everest on Difficult, Dangerous Lhotse Shar

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (594 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, jost Kobusch of Germany has moved to the Khumbu Valley to finish his acclimatization before attempting to solo winter Everest, beginning on December 22.
  • Kobusch is now in Chukhung village, from which he climbed 6,165m Island Peak (Imja Tse) yesterday.
  • Kobusch’s climb on Island Peak as shown in his tracker today.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, jost Kobusch of Germany has moved to the Khumbu Valley to finish his acclimatization before attempting to solo winter Everest, beginning on December 22. His preparations include reaching 8,000m on a different peak.

Kobusch is now in Chukhung village, from which he climbed 6,165m Island Peak (Imja Tse) yesterday. He spent the night at 6,000m, topped out again today, and went back down, as shown in his live tracker. He told ExplorersWeb that he will now rest for a few days in Lukla and then hike up the valley again to inspect conditions on his next acclimatization goal: the difficult Lhotse Shar (8,383m).

Kobusch’s climb on Island Peak as shown in his tracker today.

“My strategy is not to summit but to tag 8,000m up its flank, before heading for Everest,” he said.

Lhotse Shar is one of the main points of the Lhotse ridge, and it is climbed from south side of the mountain, with Chukhung as the starting point. The main options are to climb the southeastern flank of the Shar itself or try a direct line up the formidable south face of Lhotse.

Neither of them is easy, and the upper sections are statistically dangerous. According to Wikipedia, Lhotse Shar has the highest fatality rate of all principal or secondary 8,000m peaks. For every two climbers who summit, one person dies attempting to.

In a recent development, lhotse and its various points, as seen from the south. Graphic by Gorskie Mapy.

The Austrian expedition that first reached the summit of Lhotse Shar (from the Southeast Ridge) in 1970 set four altitude camps, the uppermost at 7,600m. They used supplemental oxygen on their summit push. “Almost the whole of the route from below Camp 1 to Camp 3 was fixed with rope, as climbing was very difficult,” they reported in the AAJ.

Kobusch will not have to deal with the nearly vertical terrain and cornices near the summit, but will have to face difficult mixed terrain and uncertain conditions if he wants to venture up to 8,000m. He will not use bottled oxygen, and as far as we know, he will climb on his own.

Kobusch plans to reach the base of Everest on December 22 and solo the mountain in winter without oxygen, via the West Ridge — the same line currently being attempted by a Russian team.

Sources indicate that this is Kobusch’s fourth attempt, and he is willing to try to reach the summit this time. However, when asked about it, he admits he does not know if such a feat is actually possible. “Every expedition, every training session, every difficult decision has been part of preparing myself for what I know will be the biggest challenge of my life,” he admits.

Kobusch’s is not the only confirmed climb this winter. Denis Urubko of Russia is reportedly preparing to climb Broad Peak in winter, possibly starting at the end of this year and continuing through January and February. On social media, Urubko mentioned he will be climbing with Vitaliy Skel. However, details of his route have not been confirmed.

Simone Moro of Italy has not decided whether to try Manaslu again this winter. He told ExplorersWeb he is still considering his prepares while observing the “crazy weather this season.” Moro attempted Manaslu in fall to acclimatize and become familiar with the terrain. However, like every other team, he had to call off the attempt due to dangerous conditions following extremely heavy snowfall. Moro wants to climb the peak in alpine style.

#67974. Tech Report: Completing The Collection

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1021 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Completing The Collection

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1021 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Completing my double hike of the AT isn’t the only commitment I am devoted to keeping.
  • Recent findings suggest that around midnight it hit me.
  • I remainder tucked under my quilt, even going so far as to eat my breakfast inside its cozy confines.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Completing my double hike of the AT isn’t the only commitment I am devoted to keeping. I check the box on another one despite a chilly morning.

Recent findings suggest that around midnight it hit me. I was camping practically at the northbound 1,200 mile marker. I hadn’t seen a marker yesterday, so it fell to me to whip one up on my way out of camp so I could my collection. This wasn’t ideal, it was barely above freezing. Every part of me wanted to stay in my tent as long as possible. When it did come time to hit the trail, I would want to get moving and stay moving, preferably all the way back to my van. My silly rituals will probably be my undoing some day.

I remainder tucked under my quilt, even going so far as to eat my breakfast inside its cozy confines. I am continually impressed how well the down insulates and warms me. I feel like I’d be warm in 20 degree weather, maybe even lower. I don’t intend to ever camp in such weather, but to know it’s possible is exactly what I had in mind when I purchased this particular quilt. It kept my warm until 7:45AM when I initiated my pack up procedure, completing the various tasks by 8:00AM, the cold having motivated me to move fast.

I checked in at the Showers Steps viewpoint since it was just a handful of steps away. It sure looked like I’d made the right choice to prioritize sunset the previous night, there wouldn’t have been much to see at sunrise given the heavy cloud cover to start the day. I located the 1,200 mile point on the trail to the tenth of a mile and swiftly pieced together a small marker. It wouldn’t last long, but I just needed a photo for my collection so I can sleep at night. I am planning to post them all in a blog post, along with other notable milestones like state lines after my hike.

In a recent development, my thin gloves were doing little to warm my fingers, but other than that I was comfortable even with the temperature sitting in the mid 30s. South of Showers Steps the trail briefly winds amongst some mountain laurels, which, unlike rocks, are in fact the state flower of Pennsylvania. A few miles later I crossed route 501 and approached the Kimmel Lookout. I spent a moment or two setting up a picture or two before whipping around and continuing down the trail. I didn’t realize it until it came time to put together today’s blog, but one of the pictures turned out kind of epic. The early morning sun radiates through clouds above speckling its light across the rocky ledge and trees. Colorful late fall trees poke up from the ground below the ledge with large meadows and farms visible further in the distance.

Early morning view from the Showers Steps.

The 1,200 mile marker, my collection is complete!

The view from the Kimmel Lookout. I think I’ll hang on to this one.

I followed the same ridge for the next 10 miles to Swatara Gap. Although it was a Saturday, it had been relatively quite on trail. I only passed a trio of hunters on the trail before encountering a lively group of women at a viewpoint along the trail. One of them had just had an interesting experience a short distance down the trail. She had stepped off the trail for a restroom break only to find out after the fact that a hunter had been just overhead on a tree stand the entire time. She didn’t seem nearly as put off by the experience as I would have been. The discussion moved to my double AT attempt. I wish I could have gotten a picture of their reaction upon hearing what I was up to. They were even more impressed that I was essentially in the final week of the task. I forgot to tell them that FarOut commenters frequently mentioned a family of 5 or so copperheads hanging out on the rocks we were all standing on, though I believe they aren’t keen on cold temperatures and were probably in hiding.

In a recent development, soon I was making my way back down to Swatara Gap and under Interstate 81. I made it the final mile back to my van before 2:00PM. After cleaning up and trimming my increasingly beardy face, I headed to Lebanon, PA to complete yesterday and today’s blog posts as has become my usual routine. There is no Formula One tomorrow so I am not sure what to do with myself, I haven’t have a Sunday morning free from blog writing or sports watching in a while. I am sure I’ll think of something.

A lookout north of Swatara Gap.

A glimpse of I-81 from the trail just north of Swatara Gap.

Passing beneath I-81 on the AT.

Total: 15.8 miles, 32,344 steps.

I’m See You Tomorrow (SYT), a 30-something hiker who loves hiking just for the thrill of seeing things that most people don’t. I have no problem eating the same things every day and, for me, over-analyzing everything is half the fun (sometimes more). I am new to backpacking but that won’t stop me from taking on an unorthodox hike of the Appalachian Trail in 2026. It’s not quite a yo-yo, but I have aspirations of hiking the entire trail twice in one year. For the rest of the story you’ll just have to start reading my blog!

#67973. The Paradox of Seeking First Ascents in Western Nepal

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1250 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

The Paradox of Seeking First Ascents in Western Nepal

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1250 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Western Nepal has plenty of unclimbed 6,000m peaks, and Fredrik Strang of Sweden and Sindre Kolbjornsgard of Norway went there planning to climb one.
  • In a recent development, what I remember most clearly about that narrow summit is not the grade, the exposure, or the possibility of being first.
  • Sindre Kolbjornsgard, left, and Fredrik Strang.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Western Nepal has plenty of unclimbed 6,000m peaks, and Fredrik Strang of Sweden and Sindre Kolbjornsgard of Norway went there planning to climb one. In the end, they settled for a slightly lower but equally memorable experience. It highlighted again that adventure goes beyond first ascents.

In a recent development, what I remember most clearly about that narrow summit is not the grade, the exposure, or the possibility of being first. It is the silence. No helicopters. No voices from a fixed-rope queue. No machinery, no aircraft, no distant sound of a settlement. Only the two of us, a serrated horizon, and an unfamiliar feeling that the mountain had asked a question rather than supplied an answer.

Sindre Kolbjornsgard, left, and Fredrik Strang. Photo: Fredrik Strang.

After 18 expeditions to 8,000’ers and witnessing the evolution (or devolution) of climbing on these peaks’ normal routes, Strang and his partner knew they wanted something different. Quoting Ed Viesturs, Strang mentioned: “The point is to climb, not just to summit.” With that in mind, the climbers set four criteria for their objectives:.

It has been revealed that several route options face the climbers’ base camp tent. Photo: Fredrik Strang.

It has been revealed that strang noted that there are many unclimbed peaks left in Nepal, but they were looking for a compelling climb, not just a dull summit for the record. They finally found one that satisfied their criteria, but then, as with so many other teams in Nepal this fall, harsh weather put their original objective out of reach. Not to mention that traveling Western Nepal is anything but simple.

According to recent reports, “Our intended destination was in the Nyalu Lek area north of Simikot,” Strang revealed. “We planned to cross Nyalu La, a pass around 5,000m, with a support party that included porters and pack animals.

Recent findings suggest that “Getting from Surkhet to Simikot took two rough days by road, with landslides having damaged or obliterated sections of the route. At Simikot, we learned that Nyalu La was probably impassable. Even reaching the place where we planned to start trekking had been uncertain.”.

According to recent reports, when they did reach the area, they confirmed that their planned peak was not an option. Hiking further down the valley, they pitched their tent at Phendol Kermi Camp. Snow had covered the trails beyond, but they simply had no time or money to move to some other region in Nepal. Instead, they decided to explore whatever was close to their camp.

During their stay, they encountered Mick Fowler and Victor Saunders of the UK. Bad weather had likewise spoiled the British pair’s plan to attempt an unclimbed 6,000m peak farther east, known only as Peak 6010, according to Mount Everest Foundation.. This would have been their second attempt on that peak. Ironically, dry conditions spoiled their 2025 attempt. This time, too much snow forced them back. Read more on the British climbers’ adventure here:.

Recent findings suggest that on October 6, Strang and Kolbjornsgard made their first acclimatization climb on a 5,177m peak at 30°20′49.82″N, 82°03′54.82″E. They found no records of any previous ascent.

It has been revealed that “From base camp, the mountain looked straightforward, and lower down, it largely was,” Strang recalls. “Steep grass, mud, and broken rock led toward the upper slopes. But at about 4,500m, the route disappeared beneath knee-deep snow, then waist-deep snow, and every step became a small excavation.”.

Industry observers note that in the following days, they scouted and flew their drone down side valleys, looking for possibilities. Their second peak was 5,227m in altitude, located at 30°07′50.86″N, 81°41′56.58″E. Again, there were no records of previous ascents. Parts of it were far from fun.

“Below 4,500m, progress was tolerable, but above that, we were back to forcing our way through knee-deep, sometimes chest-deep snow,” Strang wrote. “A tremendous amount of work for very little enjoyment.”.

Luckily, the climb improved once they reached the summit ridge, on relatively easy mixed rock and ice, which they assessed at PD+.

It has been revealed that “Fowler and Saunders climbed the mountain several days later and found an easier way to descend and reascend the step on its western side,” Strang noted. “Their solution was a reminder that the first line a team takes is not necessarily the best one.”.

Still, the peak that most drew the climbers’ attention was a remarkable 5,337m tooth of rock above Yangchya Lake at approximately 30°07′09.36″N, 81°41′21.15″E.

“We began calling it Daara Peak — a name inspired by the Nepali word for a projecting tooth or fang and by the mountain’s striking shape,” Strang mentioned. He notes that the name is provisional while they await a response from the authorities about their suggestion.

It has been revealed that strang describes the peak as “a saber-toothed tiger’s canine protruding from a mass of rock. The terminal pinnacle was about eight meters high, overhanging and sharply defined against the sky.”.

The climbers about to reach what they called Daara Peak. Drone photo: Brizendra Bhattarai.

Industry observers note that the problem was approaching the peak in deep, heavy snow from Yangchya Lake. They failed on their first attempt to tackle its northeast headwall. After waiting out another snowy spell, the climbers returned for a second attempt on October 17-18.

The climbers dealt with 250m of rather poor rock, a complex approach to the headwall across a bergschrund with soft snow, and the uncertainty of moving on unfamiliar terrain. They had no idea of the difficulties ahead or whether they could protect the passages ahead on their way to the summit. The route included vertical granite walls, with cracks adequate for cams, some mixed terrain with the crux at M6, a steep couloir, and then the summit ridge: a granite edge with some 30cm of snow on top.

Climbing terrain on Daara Peak. Photo: Fredrik Strang.

Sources indicate that rather than technical difficulty, the section was delicate due to exposure and a lack of comfortable belay stations. Yet, the climbers reached the summit on October 18, including the top of the final pinnacle, thanks to a crack in the rock.

Strang admits that the climbing details suggest a rather straightforward ascent: a 5,337m summit via its northeast side in five pitches with difficulties up to M6. However, Strang judges the climb on a different scale. “The technical crux was behind us, but it was the part I remember most vividly,” he explained. “It was the silence.”.

According to recent reports, strang and Kolbjornsgard’s route up Daara Peak. Photo: Fredrik Strang.

Industry observers note that on many of the 8,000m peaks I have climbed, the human presence has become part of the landscape: camps, radio calls, fixed ropes, queues, and the distant sound of aircraft. Up here, none of that reached us. Mountains extended in every direction. There was no audience, no ceremony, no one to confirm that we had accomplished anything at all.

Industry observers note that strang also reflects on the paradox: They enjoyed the wild terrain but, if every climber chases solitude by visiting these last remote valleys, the character of these places will inevitably change. For Strang, the question is not to ban access. However, he says:.

Perhaps some summits should remain untouched — not because we lack the skill or courage to reach them, but because future generations deserve to inherit mountains that have not all been reduced to objectives.

The climb from the ridge. Photo: Fredrik Strang.

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (931 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

A Night with a Camino Ghost

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (931 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that we slept surprisingly well last night, even though our room sat directly above a lively bar.
  • Industry observers note that with the window shutters closed, we blocked out all the street noise.
  • It has been revealed that this morning, I walked out to the kitchen and opened the tall doors leading to the courtyard to let the cool air in.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that we slept surprisingly well last night, even though our room sat directly above a lively bar. People partied and ate dinner late into the night. That is completely normal here, as most businesses close for siesta and do not reopen until after 8:00 PM.

Industry observers note that with the window shutters closed, we blocked out all the street noise. Unfortunately, closing them also trapped the heat inside, making the room quite warm.

It has been revealed that this morning, I walked out to the kitchen and opened the tall doors leading to the courtyard to let the cool air in. I made a cup of coffee and ate fresh blueberries with yogurt.

Because it was Sunday morning, the street noise was minimal. Listening to the seagulls and mourning doves while sipping coffee was a peaceful way to start the day.

We finally set off at 9:00 AM. Pontevedra is a good-sized city with an intact medieval center, so it took us a little while to walk out of town. Before long, however, we found ourselves back on a quiet country road.

Sources indicate that the Camino wound alongside a river before merging onto a paved road. We took the road route, which was poorly marked, but we soon reconnected with the main trail. Along the way, we passed hundreds of pilgrims heading in the opposite direction toward Santiago.

In a recent development, from there, the trail entered the woods and began to climb. It got quite steep for a short stretch before leveling out into a pleasant forest path. We hiked downhill over rocky terrain, passing cool, shaded creeks along the way.

Eventually, we emerged into Pontesampaio, a well-kept medieval village. We wound our way through its narrow alleyways down to a wide river. To cross, we had to wait our turn on a narrow, 300-foot arched stone bridge, letting oncoming cars pass before we walked across.

Once across, we stopped at a local restaurant serving ultra-fresh food. I ordered grilled squid that had just come off the docks that morning, and the restaurant even harvests its own chickens. Best of all, the meal was a fraction of what it would cost back in the States.

After a relaxing siesta lunch, we still had about 7.5 kilometers (4.6 miles) left to hike.

As we walked through several connected medieval neighborhoods, the Camino suddenly split into two routes:.

At first, the split confused me, and seeing the mountain crest ahead was intimidating because we were already hot and tired. Fortunately, we chose the shorter Coastal route, and the trail skirted the side of the mountain rather than going straight over the top.

However, the descent brought us onto the shoulder of a busy highway. We endured two miserable miles of roaring traffic and exhaust fumes before finally reaching Redondela.

Redondela felt a bit rundown in spots, though it features a charming medieval quarter beneath a massive, 100-foot-tall iron train trestle.

Sources indicate that we arrived at our apartment at 4:00 PM, completely exhausted. Our host was wonderful and had prepared a special herbal tea for us to soak our feet. The recipe belonged to his grandmother, who was actually the very first pharmacist in Redondela. (Unlike in the States, pharmacists in Spain can prescribe and dispense many medications without a doctor’s visit.).

It has been revealed that while soaking our feet, we drank some mediocre Spanish wine. Because it was Sunday afternoon, almost everything was closed except for a small mini-market with limited options.

In a recent development, later, we visited a local bakery our host recommended. Hikers always love talking about food—when you are burning thousands of calories a day, you promptly get tired of trail snacks and start dreaming about town food. We loaded up on a few local treats:.

After the bakery, we wandered through the narrow alleyways of the old city, admiring the elevated rail bridge towering overhead. By 8:00 PM, the town came alive as bars and restaurants reopened after siesta.

This time, the waitress brought out two small bowls of white noodles soaked in olive oil with bread on the side. The noodles had dark streaks of squid ink running down them, adding a mild, salty seafood flavor.

In a recent development, exhausted from the long walk, we headed back to the apartment. Our host had preserved the space just as his grandmother left it—it truly felt like she still lived there. We threw the windows wide open to let the cool night air roll in and fell fast asleep, though it felt like Grandma’s presence lingered in the room all night long.

The buyer pays the same price as they would otherwise, and your purchase helps to support The Trek's ongoing goal to serve you quality backpacking advice and information. Thanks for your support!

To learn more, please visit the About This Site page.

Sources indicate that after decades of no backpacking an abrupt life incident forced me back into the woods for some shinrin-yoku where I ran into a NOBO tramily at Shuckstack Fire Tower. That started an idea of a longer term forest bath on the AT. What a long strange trip its been. Any financial donations I get will be used to send out love to other thru hikers a trail magic.
