#67971. A Climbing Expedition to 'Central Asia's Patagonia'

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1948 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

A Climbing Expedition to 'Central Asia's Patagonia'

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1948 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A mix of nine young and veteran Croatian climbers spent the month of August in one of the world’s great big-wall destinations — Kyrgyzstan’s Karavshin Range in the Pamir-Alay Mountains.
  • According to recent reports, the two leaders, Sinisa Skalec and Lukas Grbac Lackovic, spoke to ExplorersWeb about the place and their expedition.
  • Though suffering from stomach challenges for most of the month (more on this later), the team repeated several granite classics, did a fresh route on 4,430m Pik Breeze, and attempted another new line.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A mix of nine young and veteran Croatian climbers spent the month of August in one of the world’s great big-wall destinations — Kyrgyzstan’s Karavshin Range in the Pamir-Alay Mountains. Reaching up to 5,509m, the once-unknown granite cliffs now draw dozens of international climbers each summer. The two core valleys, Ak-Su and Kara-Su, have become known as Central Asia’s Patagonia.

According to recent reports, the two leaders, Sinisa Skalec and Lukas Grbac Lackovic, spoke to ExplorersWeb about the place and their expedition. First, a summary of their four weeks.

Though suffering from stomach challenges for most of the month (more on this later), the team repeated several granite classics, did a fresh route on 4,430m Pik Breeze, and attempted another new line.

Recent findings suggest that three climbers — Bruno Crljenic, Eva Pejic, and Lackovic — identified a potential newly introduced line below Pik Breeze’s west ridge. They knew of only one previous route on the mountain, done by Russians Marina Popova and Denis Prokofiev.

Crossing a scree slope on Pik Breeze.

Beginning at 5am, the three crossed a broad scree slope, then began climbing a couloir below Pik Breeze’s west ridge. They negotiated loose rock, briefly followed an existing line, then moved left into crack systems.

Canned Horse, 6c A0, top. Below, previous attempts and possible other lines on the face.

They climbed until 9pm, when they bivouacked on a tiny ledge with space for only two people sitting and one lying down. Resuming at 8:30am, they reached a col after three pitches and continued directly up slabs and cracks. They finished on easier IV/V terrain and followed a 200m ridge to the summit.

Industry observers note that they called their fresh line Canned Horse, 930m, 23 pitches, 6c A0. It took them a further eight hours to get back to base camp. During the climb, they found pitons on two pitches. They believe these belonged to another route on the west ridge, but the history of that line, and whether it was finished, is uncertain.

Pejic, Grbac Lackovic, and Crljenic on top of Pik Breeze.

Later in the month, one of those climbers, Eva Pejic, became quite ill and couldn’t leave base camp on her own. Five teammates helped evacuate her, carrying her for 11km, with assistance from other climbers in the area. She later recuperated in the Kyrgyz city of Osh.

On the first crux of ‘Perestroika Crack.’.

Three small teams of Croatian climbers also repeated Perestroika Crack, one of the best-known long granite routes in Central Asia. It rises about 900m up the north face of 4,240m Pik Slesova and is graded 7a. Three members reportedly free-climbed the route. One pair, Sinisa Skalec and Ivan Vitez, completed the line in a single marathon day, beginning at 5:45am, summiting at 5:40pm, and returning to base camp at 11pm.

According to recent reports, skalec and Vitez also repeated the French Ridge of 4,510m Kyrkchilta, 2,000m, 6b to 6b+. They needed one bivouac. Toward the end of August, this same pair attempted a first ascent on the Central Pyramid of Ortotyubek, overlooking base camp. Their attempted route mounted slabs and cracks to the left of the established Take It Easy line, which other Croatians had repeated during that month. The pair gave up their attempt on August 26 because of illness.

Base camp with Ortotyubek and Slesova in the background.

Here is our interview with Lukas Grbac Lackovic and Sinisa Skalec about Kyrgyzstan and the Ak-Su Valley.

Lukas Grbac Lackovic repeats the Central Route on a peak called Small Russian Tower.

Was Eva Pejic’s health problem related to altitude or something else? What was the illness you experienced on Ortotyubek?

Eva’s health problem was unrelated to altitude exposure or the expedition environment. However, most of us experienced gastrointestinal infections, with symptoms including diarrhea, bloating, fever, and general malaise.

This significantly hindered our climbing, as everyone in the team got sick at least once, and some even twice. Recovery was slow and never quite complete –- we felt weak for most of the trip.

One thing that helped us recover was having plain rice with some of our meals, which we could get from the cook if we asked nicely. If we were to go again, we would definitely bring our own food and cooking equipment. This can be inconvenient, but it could potentially save you at least a week of being sick and unable to climb.

Another view of base camp and peaks Ortotyubek and Slesova.

It has been revealed that can you describe the Karavshin Valley? How large is it? Are there many side valleys?

The two main valleys are Ak-Su and Kara-Su. Adjacent to them is the Jaupaya Valley, which provides a descent route from Pik Breeze and is home to several peaks around 5,000m high. The rock quality there appears poor, and we are not aware of any established rock routes in the valley.

It has been revealed that another interesting area, west of Kara Su, is the Orto-Chashma Gorge. An Italian team made a first ascent there during our visit.

Here in the West, we first heard about the area following the kidnapping of four American climbers in Kara-Su in 2000. Since then, it seems to have calmed down and become a popular climbing destination. Is the area considered safe nowadays, or are there still things climbers should be aware of?

In a recent development, currently, the security situation in the valley is good. There is always the possibility of tensions, of course, as the valleys lie close to the border with Tajikistan. However, in recent years, the number of climbers visiting the area has increased exponentially, reaching around 100 climbers this year.

Industry observers note that how many other climbing teams were in Ak-Su and neighboring Kara-Su while you were there? Where were they generally from?

Industry observers note that during the three weeks we spent in the valley, up to 50 climbers were in BC at the same time. Climbers came from all over the world — Chile, U.S., Spain, Slovakia, Poland, Belgium, Slovenia, France, Italy, Germany, Japan, Russia….

Why did your group decide to go there?

It has been revealed that we had originally planned a different expedition, but had to change our destination just a few months before departure. Some friends from Croatia and Slovenia recommended the area because of its straightforward logistics and relatively good security, while still offering impressive substantial walls and proper crack climbing. It didn’t take much to convince us!

Are there any military checkpoints? Do you need special permission to enter the valleys?

Yes, you have to pass through a military checkpoint when entering the area. However, the outfitter handles the application for the necessary permits and ensures everything goes smoothly.

Some call the Karavshin Valley the Patagonia of Central Asia because of its aesthetic granite walls. Do you think that’s a fair description?

Patagonia is definitely more spectacular, but you pay the price with poor weather. If your goal is to climb almost every day, then the Karavshin Valley is a better choice.

Climbing in Patagonia requires much more logistical planning and preparation, and the approaches themselves are a whole different story. In the Karavshin Valley, on the other hand, there is no snow or ice during the season we visited (August), at least on the walls we climbed. Some of the walls are just a 15-minute walk from BC, and you can reach them all in approach shoes.

Perestroika Crack and some of the classic routes in the Karavshin region are arguably just as good as the best rock routes in Patagonia.

How does the granite compare to Yosemite and Patagonia?

The granite is more similar in texture to that found in Patagonia; it is not as smooth as in Yosemite. The overall rock quality is generally good, although, as everywhere, some sections are of poorer quality. One downside of the mild climate in the Karavshin Valley is the dirt and grass that accumulate in the cracks, which can sometimes detract from the aesthetic appeal of the routes. The more popular and frequently climbed routes have already been cleaned and are pleasant to climb.

Sources indicate that you climbed 4-1/2 pitches of the route on Ortotyubek. How much did you have left to complete it?

Sources indicate that there were still two-and-a-half pitches left to complete the route up to the junction with Take It Easy. We envisioned the second half of the fifth pitch following the line up to a point just below the overhang that runs diagonally to the left.

From there, the sixth pitch follows a thin crack, from which you need to traverse left and move into another system of thin cracks that runs across the roof and joins the Take It Easy belay (seventh pitch). The last pitch of Take It Easy offers a logical exit, and we don’t think there is any need to come up with an alternative.

At the point where we stopped (first half of the fifth pitch), we left two pitons that we used as a temporary rappel anchor. Repeating parties are welcome to remove them, as they were only left for temporary use. We think a few bolts may be needed in the second half of the fifth pitch, but that obviously depends on the abilities of those planning to complete the route.

All belays are equipped (the first and fourth belays have two 8mm bolts each, while the second and third have two pitons each). In addition, we left two or three pitons in the first pitch and two in the second pitch.

In a recent development, as in the rest of the valley, some sections of the route are filled with dirt and grass. We made an effort to clean the cracks in the first four pitches, but there is still plenty of work to be done, especially on the sixth pitch, which we didn’t climb, where a thin crack is completely filled with dirt.

How much unclimbed rock remains? Are the obvious lines already established, or are there still many promising routes?

The most obvious and accessible lines may have already been climbed, but there is still plenty of potential. Anyone willing to put in the effort can establish a new route. The area is vast, and there is still plenty of room for new routes.

It has been revealed that your website mentions that there are guidebooks to certain routes in that area. Where are these available?

It has been revealed that most of the guidebooks we used are available online. We received some Russian guidebooks from climbing friends, although we didn’t use them very much. We’re not sure how easily they can be found online. Climbers from all over the world bring various materials to the camp, so most route topos and information can be obtained there.

What was the most unexpected experience on your expedition — something that might surprise climbers familiar with other significant-wall areas?

Recent findings suggest that we were pleasantly surprised by the kindness and honesty of the Kyrgyz people. When traveling to remote parts of the world, many of us tend to expect that someone will try to rip us off and that we will have to haggle over everything, but that was not the case here.

Although some things took longer than expected, everything we had agreed on in advance was respected, and all the logistics for transportation and accommodation worked very well.

As we mentioned earlier, our only complaint concerns the food and hygiene conditions at the camp, which were most likely responsible for the digestive problems experienced by virtually all the climbers staying there.

#67965. Latest Update: Day 38: The Last Full Day Before Santiago

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1081 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Day 38: The Last Full Day Before Santiago

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1081 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Knowing it was the last major walking day before Santiago, I got up early and started under the stars.
  • The shadow of the trees made it nearly impossible to see where I was going, but I leaned into the challenge.
  • I wove in and out of towns, trying to find a cafe that was open, but every single one I passed was closed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Knowing it was the last major walking day before Santiago, I got up early and started under the stars.

The shadow of the trees made it nearly impossible to see where I was going, but I leaned into the challenge.

My legs had been consistently sore for a week.

And yet, I didn’t want to stop walking.

As the sun came up, though, so did my mood.

I wove in and out of towns, trying to find a cafe that was open, but every single one I passed was closed. Many of the restaurants and albergues were closing for the season. In a way, it felt like we were politely being asked to “wrap it up.”.

Well, a beautiful stone-walled restaurant was my savior. The WiFi network was called “A Cova de Meiga” (a cove of the witch), and it felt like a warm sanctuary.

A fire in the corner, old sewing machines and instruments on the wall, and the restaurant owner’s two young boys brought a childlike joy to my morning.

My Argentinian brother found me there and we shared a tarta de Santiago with our coffees as we warmed up by the fire.

After that cafe, we made it two kilometers before we found our Italian brother at another cafe.

He asked if we wanted anything, and even though we all had just stopped, I suggested we get another coffee and take the day very slowly.

They were more than happy with that idea, and we all sat with another round of café con leche while we shared a tortilla.

When we started walking, silence quickly became the conversation.

The presence of the moment felt potent as we saw the trail markers giving a countdown.

Each leaf glowing with the wind.

The smell of pine from the needles I crushed in my hand.

The chill of the wind combined with the warmth of the sun.

Every detail felt more vibrant because it was the last full day.

Recent findings suggest that in O Pedrouzo, we decided to stop again for lunch. With a table full of food at the Mexican restaurant, A Catriña, we talked and ate and talked and ate.

There were still 15 out of the 36 kilometers to do, so together we set out into the afternoon sun.

Recent findings suggest that we walked through what felt like a magical forest, with everything around us was alive with the most intense colors of green. Like little kids, we hugged the trees, climbed them, and hung from their bark.

According to recent reports, once we hit the trail marker that read we were under ten kilometers, I saw my Italian brother put a sticker on the column. I stopped next to him and he suggested we walk together till the end. In agreement, I plopped on the road to wait for our third. A few minutes later, our Argentinian brother jumped on us in greeting. We lay there in that spot, soaking up the reality of being so close to Santiago.

Together, side-by-side-by-side, we finished the last stretch of the day. Our strides naturally matching, we marched onward, each taking turns singing our country’s national anthems. It felt like our individual patriotism fed the energy of the group. The exact energy boost we needed for the end.

At the municipal albergue in Monte de Gozo, the Pilgrims Hostel was basically a compound. We were in a building labeled 29, and the others were in a terraced line down the descent. They were newly constructed, and there were enough to fit 400 pilgrims. We only ended up with 9 pilgrims on the whole property.

Nearby at the pilgrim monument overlooking Santiago, the three of us caught the sunset at the perfect time as it was about to go over the horizon. I couldn’t believe I was looking at the cathedral that we’d talked about for so long. Leaning against the metal monument, I cried for the end of the journey.

Tomorrow, I’d touch that cathedral.

Industry observers note that sitting on the hill, I realized I felt more present and at peace today than I had for most of my life. Then it hit me….

Those had been my intentions for the year, and tomorrow starts a new cycle of intentions.

Our last full night was spent making a steep descent to the grocery store just to climb back up and eat.

Industry observers note that our Italian brother entertained the pilgrims in the kitchen. He ate hot dogs raw while he cooked fish sticks in the microwave, initially thinking they were chicken and didn’t need to be fried. They did need to be fried.

One of the girls from Germany had been carrying a candle for her whole Camino. She had only used it once, but in celebration of my upcoming birthday, she lit it and set it in front of me to make a pre-birthday wish. How special.

Once everyone was done eating, we played Uno with seven people. The four other people had walked different Caminos (the Primitivo and the Norte) and weren’t as accustomed to the crowds. To us, the numbers in the albergue were few, so getting to hear different stories and perspectives was fascinating.

Sources indicate that I laughed the perfect amount for the last night. It was joyful.

#67964. Industry News: Avalanche Fatality Warns About Early Ski Conditions In The Alps

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (813 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Avalanche Fatality Warns About Early Ski Conditions In The Alps

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (813 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, little snow on the mountains doesn’t mean safe conditions.
  • Industry observers note that with the ski season barely underway, this is Europe’s first avalanche victim this season.
  • Industry observers note that most victims perished in the Alps: 40 in Italy, 35 in France, 33 in Austria, and 18 in Switzerland.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, little snow on the mountains doesn’t mean safe conditions. An American off-piste skier died in the Austrian Alps last weekend after he triggered a small slab avalanche. It was far too small to bury him, but it carried him into an open crevasse below.

Industry observers note that with the ski season barely underway, this is Europe’s first avalanche victim this season. Last year, 151 people died in avalanches in Europe between October 2025 and June 2026, according to the European Avalanche Warning Service (EAWS), a shockingly high number.

Industry observers note that most victims perished in the Alps: 40 in Italy, 35 in France, 33 in Austria, and 18 in Switzerland. It was the 13th most deadly year in the Alps since record-keeping began. It was also the highest tally ever since the “Winter of Terror” of 1951. Avalanche prevention standards have improved a lot since then, but the number of leisure skiers, climbers, and hikers in the mountains has multiplied as well. (Most of those 1951 victims lived in villages along avalanche paths.).

Last weekend’s accident took place at the Stubai Glacier ski resort. The glacier sections of the Alps typically open for skiing weeks earlier than other mountain resorts, thanks to their higher altitudes and glacial ice, which can provide good October skiing with just a thin layer of fresh snow on top. Stubai’s ski resort opened on October 9 this year.

A map of Stubai Glacier ski resort with the area where the accident happened circled in red. Photo: Stubaier Gletscher website.

It has been revealed that the skier was on his own, descending in an out-of-bounds area below East Daunkogel Peak at around 11:30am. His tracks on the snow show he eventually abandoned the snow-covered glacier and ventured onto a steeper, rocky area. At some point, he broke a small slab of crusty snow which dragged him some 50 meters into an open bergschrund, where he fatally fell 20 meters down, according to the Lawinen Report.

Industry observers note that the accident site, with the skier’s tracks visible,  and the movement of the snow slab — 50m long and 25m wide — marked in pink. Photo: Lawinen Report.

It has been revealed that other skiers in the area saw the accident and raised the alarm, but the skier had died by the time they extracted him from the crevasse. The police stated the slab was only 10cm to 30cm thick, and the slide was just 25 meters wide. The crevasse was 50 meters below the fracture point.

Avalanche risks are obvious on heavily loaded slopes, but the accident shows that even a thin layer of unstable snow can cause a fatal fall. In this case, the snow had fallen recently on the verglass ice over glacier-polished smooth rocks, and had no time to settle. This is a typical early-season condition in mountain ranges around the world.

In a recent development, the accident occurred at nearly 3,000m of altitude on a shady northeast slope, where the snow hardly transforms and settles during the short days of late fall. To make things worse, the report notes that wind had picked up that morning, creating a weak crust on top of loose, cold, fresh snow, prone to breaking.

According to recent reports, the avalanche site on the following day, with most of the terrain covered by freshly drifted snow. Photo: LWD Tirol.

According to recent reports, the second factor was exposure: the skier might have easily survived the fall if the terrain had been a clean snow slope, but he was on rocky terrain, where a simple fall can result in serious injuries. Most of all, the crevasse below created what the report described as a “terrain trap.”.

It has been revealed that fans of backcountry and ski touring are eager to hit the slopes with the first snowflakes, and the scarcely covered terrain may provide a false sense of safety from avalanches. But objective dangers go beyond the major powder avalanches and also include falls on icy slopes. In addition, the glaciers are dry after the summer, and the crevasses are wide open.

In a recent development, after a mild fall, snow is falling heavily in the Alps this week, significantly improving conditions for the region’s ski resorts. Most of them initiative to open this weekend. The snow will also offer backcountry opportunities, but conditions will remain highly unstable.

Snowfall up to two meters is expected today in the Alps. Graphic by meteoexploration.com.

The avalanche report today by the Tiroler Avalanche Service (LWD Tirol) indicates low risk in the Austrian mountains, a remarkable risk (3 out of 5) in the Swiss Alps, and moderate risk (2 out of 5) in France.

The avalanche forecast for today, November 19, in the Alps shows remarkable (level 3-orange) risk, especially in Switzerland. Graphic: LWD Tirol.

  • Sources indicate that today, November 19, the Yamanashi Prefectural Police announced that they had ended the search for Chinese climber Chen Jie, 25, according to the Japanese national newspaper Mainichi Shimbun.
  • His two companions reportedly turned back because of deteriorating weather and inadequate equipment.
  • His father subsequently traveled to Japan and offered a reward of RMB500,000 ($75,000) for information leading to his recovery alive, or RMB100,000 ($15,000) for recovery of his body.

Sources indicate that today, November 19, the Yamanashi Prefectural Police announced that they had ended the search for Chinese climber Chen Jie, 25, according to the Japanese national newspaper Mainichi Shimbun. Chen disappeared November 8 on the main Yoshida Trail after continuing alone up 3,776m Mount Fuji during its closed season.

His two companions reportedly turned back because of deteriorating weather and inadequate equipment. Chen continued on his own without crampons or sufficient cold-weather clothing. His last video was sent that morning between 2,300 and 2,700m.

His father subsequently traveled to Japan and offered a reward of RMB500,000 ($75,000) for information leading to his recovery alive, or RMB100,000 ($15,000) for recovery of his body.

Ironically, Chen belonged to China’s Blue Sky Rescue Team, a volunteer search-and-rescue organization. His mother told local media that he had participated in rescues in China and had some mountaineering experience, including trekking and climbing in Nepal and Indonesia.

#67954. New Mexico is the reward

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1826 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

New Mexico is the reward

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1826 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The library is a bit chaotic, all the books are in the process of being boxed up for a move.
  • According to recent reports, I wanted to do some blogging but turns out the library closes for lunch.
  • In true CDT fashion its covered in barbed wire and bones!
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The library is a bit chaotic, all the books are in the process of being boxed up for a move. I ask when they are moving and where to. The librarian doesn’t know herself. There are two computers there which Brokeback and i jump on to fill out our NDA permit forms. There isn’t any clear guidance on how to fill them out, so we call Fort Huachua and ask some questions. The person who answers say i need to have an active service member, veteran or DOD contractor as a sponsor. This doesn’t seem to add up to what the CDTC claims about international hikers, we just need to be with a US citizen who also had the permit. So i skip this on the form. We go into a back room with whitish walls to take pictures  for the permit. Mine is pretty bad! I compile all the documents and send everything off to the Fort Huachuca email. Fingers crossed!

According to recent reports, I wanted to do some blogging but turns out the library closes for lunch. Brokeback and i walk back into town. Chama is a pretty long town that stretches along the road, so its a while. I drop into the grocery store to get more of my resupply. There i meet Tim & Cassie again. They are staying with JJ and invite me to come over for a dinner they are cooking. I say yes, and after finishing we walk back into town. We spend the afternoon hanging out with the rest of the Oysters outside the Iron Rail Inn. Later we walk over to JJ’s with Tim & Cassie. There we make dinner together and chat for a good while. I also get to peek around the Exoticpax  and Aardwolf production rooms. Its pretty cool getting to see their setups as someone who also makes gear.

In true CDT fashion its covered in barbed wire and bones!

The dusk sky near Lagunitas lake.

Groves of golden Aspen were very common on this part of the trail.

Its pretty cold overnight, and at about 5am I’m awake. There’s frost on the ground and so after heading off to dig my morning cathole, i decide to pack up and start hiking in the dark. I reach the edge of the mesa we are on shortly after dawn and am treated to views of the pine forests below.

Looking down towards Abiquiu in the morning.

After this the trail descends down towards Ghost Ranch and pretty promptly the landscape changes from pine forest to something more arid. Its when we reach the Arroyo del Yeso that we get our first true sense of being in the desert!

Our first true view of the Upcoming Mexico desert near Ghost Ranch.

Sources indicate that every September Albuquerque hosts the hot air balloon fiesta. Back in Chama we decided to go if we could get tickets. Its a couple of hours drive, through a desert landscape. I look around as we drive and wonder if this is what the rest of Upcoming Mexico is going to be like.

Recent findings suggest that we get tickets for the morning session, so wake up at about 4am the next day. I feel pretty awful on the short car ride over. By the time we are walking into the Arena i start to feel pretty excited, and after getting coffee i feel pretty good. I imagined we would be in a viewing area away from the balloon. However you get to walk in among them as they set up which was so cool! The first balloons lifted off just before sunrise to the strains of the US National Anthem. After this its was a constant stream of balloons being inflated and lifting off! There must have been around 100 balloons in the air at one point. 2027 SOBO’s, this is one amazing sidequest!

The first balloons lifting off before dawn.

After leaving the festival we got breakfast and then napped back at the hotel. Did some laundry and just hung out for the rest of the day. Later we drove to an all you can eat sushi restaurant and demolished many rolls!

Sources indicate that while visiting Albuqerque had been fun, it was definitely a little overwhelming to be in such a massive city. So i was glad to be heading back to trail. Tengram dropped us off at Ghost Ranch around midday. He was going to camp with us that evening so we put camping bits in his car and get slacked again.

The crew hiking out towards the Rio Chama.

In a recent development, the route out of Ghost Ranch is pretty nice, and goes on a piece of the land that you usually don’t get to access. Now there were substantial sandstone cliffs in almost all directions and it felt like we were truly in the desert. We crossed the highway and followed the dirt road up alongside the Rio Chama towards where the Ghost Ranch Alt rejoins the redline. Halfway along there is a campsite where Tengram is setup. We gather for dinner and then the projector comes out for the Second Twilight Movie! I enjoy it in a its so bad its good kind of way.

Industry observers note that the others in the Oysters were going to do a backyard ultra to Cuba the next day, about 50 miles. I decided that this wasn’t really for me, i always prefer a more even split of days over doing an epic one and zeroing to recover. So after the film had finished i set off. It started to rain pretty soon after i set off. At first a little bit but gets pretty heavy. Walking down the dirt road in the dark and rain makes me wonder if i should have stayed and camped with the others. In the end i hike for an hour or so to rejoin the CDT redline and make a little progress. By the time i find somewhere to camp the rain has stopped. There is a little tree with some pine duff which isn’t too damp.

Recent findings suggest that I’m woken up before by the Oysters passing as they start their ultra. While i’m not planning on hiking 50 miles, i still need to do a pretty massive day if i want to catch up with them in Cuba. So i pack up and set off in the dark. The sunrise over the cliffs is pretty nice and the trail is kind of chill for a bit.

Sources indicate that it follows a small stream in a shallow canyon before climbing up to a mesa. Here the trail has really been washed out by the heavy rain. The water has scoured out the streambed a good 4 or 5 feet in places, and there are areas where flood debris has been jammed up against trees. The result is a constant climbing in and out of the streambed trying to follow the trail. Its pretty tiring and I’m almost glad when i leave and get to climb up onto the Mesa.

According to recent reports, from there the trail continues up high before dropping down towards a highway. Looking out over the landscape i realize that before i know it this journey will be over. I have a little bittersweet cry on my way down.

In a recent development, one thing this trail does is constantly surprise me with the landscapes. In my head Newly introduced Mexico is an entire state like The Great Divide Basin. Climbing up into The San Luis Parks Wilderness area it feels a little bit like I’m back in Colorado. There are loads of aspens and wide open meadowy spaces. I stop around sunset for dinner, then keep hiking into the dark. Its a little spooky, especially when i see hunters our with their headtorches on. I also go the wrong way for about a mile and have to turn back.

Eventually i  pass the San Gregoria Reservoir and come to the southern boundary of the Wilderness area. Here there is a trailhead with pit toilet, where i find a flattish spot to camp. Im pretty tired and Its only another 20km into Cuba, which is all downhill and i should be able to easily do in the morning.

In the morning i set off from the trailhead and start descending. There are some cow paths and i end up paralleling the CDT for a while, and have to do a little bushwhack back to the path. As the trail descends the trees open up, the groundcover gets sparser and it feels more arid. Soon the trail leaves the trees and comes to a little overlook. From here i can see out to Cuba. Now it feels like i am truly in the desert!

Recent findings suggest that the rest of the way into Cuba is along dirt roads. Cuba is pretty notorious for loose dogs that sometimes come out and bite hikers. There are plenty of tales of hikers having to get stitches from bites. I’ll admit that dogs scare me a little bit, and so i pretty alert on my way in. Close to town there was a house with a couple of dogs outside, who barked at me, but otherwise stayed put.

It has been revealed that in Cuba i reunite with the Oysters at one of the motels there around lunchtime. I do my town chores while we watch Tombstone and drink Coors Banquets. Later we head down to a cafe to get dinner. While we are eating a man comes over. His name is Jim and he does trail maintenance on the CDT around the area, and talks to us about our hike. Then notes that he’s settled up the bill for us! A nice and much welcomed surprise.

According to recent reports, this first week in New Mexico has been such a nice change in the nature of the hike. Without the need to push massive days hanging over me, I feel like I can relax and really enjoy this last part of the hike.

#67937. Climbers Forge New Route on Mount Shiva Despite Limited Acclimatization

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Climbers Forge New Route on Mount Shiva Despite Limited Acclimatization

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (622 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Benjamin Bosshard and Philippo Sala will never forget their first experience above 6,000m and the fresh route they opened with Stefan Siegrist on India’s Bahai Jar, commonly known as Mount Shiva (6,142m).
  • Recent findings suggest that expeditions in the Indian Himalaya are usually quiet while they take place, because satellite phones and InReach devices are prohibited.
  • According to recent reports, siegrist had already visited the Chenab River Valley area in 2018 and climbed Shiva with Jonas Schild, but he still had designs on its unclimbed northwest ridge.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Benjamin Bosshard and Philippo Sala will never forget their first experience above 6,000m and the fresh route they opened with Stefan Siegrist on India’s Bahai Jar, commonly known as Mount Shiva (6,142m).

Recent findings suggest that expeditions in the Indian Himalaya are usually quiet while they take place, because satellite phones and InReach devices are prohibited. After returning home, however, Stefan Siegrist reported the details, and the team’s cameraman, Christoph Detschmann, posted a video summary of the expedition:.

According to recent reports, siegrist had already visited the Chenab River Valley area in 2018 and climbed Shiva with Jonas Schild, but he still had designs on its unclimbed northwest ridge. At the end of September, he, Sala, and Bosshard reached base camp in the Kishtwar massif.

The three Swiss climbers were prepared to endure a long period of bad weather while acclimatizing. To their surprise, a good weather window opened right away. It was too good to let go, despite not being properly acclimatized and Sala and Bosshard’s lack of altitude experience. The window was expected to last just three days. After many “discussions and doubts,” they left base camp on October 3.

Sala had a headache during the first night, but the following morning, they were all totally focused on the climb, and the tension disappeared. “We assumed that we were unlikely to reach the summit on this attempt, and that we would therefore be wasting our only chance before a major storm [brought] the season to an end,” Siegrist explained. “So from then on, the idea was simply to climb higher and acclimatize, without any pressure.”.

A moment of the climb, filmed from a drone by Christoph Detschmann.

According to recent reports, along the way, they discovered they had left their stove at base camp. No problem in 2026: The expedition photographer used his drone to carry the stove up to them. The use of drones was a hot topic during the recent Piolets d’Or: To what extent are they compatible with alpine-style criteria? While most accepted that drones could scout routes or sections out of view of base camp, many considered using them to carry equipment up a face to be a red line.

On Shiva, Siegrist claims the delivery of the missing stove “proved essential to the success of the climb.”.

It has been revealed that the climbers spent their second night at 5,250m at the base of the northwest ridge. On the following morning, they had to decide whether to continue or retreat. They all felt well, but starting the highly technical ridge was a point of no return. At the same time, Siegrist recalls, they realized they really had a chance to summit. And so on they went.

According to recent reports, that night, they stopped at 5,700m in what Siegrist describes as a crucial moment. His partners had not been at that altitude before, and the latest forecast confirmed a storm the following day. They decided to wait and see what the morning looked like. No one slept at all that night.

Industry observers note that the last meters before the summit. Drone image by Christoph Detschmann.

Recent findings suggest that the sky was still clear when the team set off again at 4am, so they chose to keep going. “After a while, we finally reached the final slope, just 300m below the summit,” Siegrist wrote. By now, they knew they were going to make it. They reached the top at 7:44am, six days after arriving in Base Camp, and just in time to hurry down as the storm approached.

The climbers descended via the 1985 Japanese route (see topo below), and reached their base camp tents as it started to snow.

#67933. The Foothills Trail – Day 0

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (720 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

The Foothills Trail – Day 0

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (720 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The morning before I was supposed to meet my shuttle driver, I haphazardly threw my pack together.
  • Sources indicate that upon arrival at the state park, I registered as a hiker and asked for a primitive campsite with no preference on location.
  • With only a 5-minute walk to camp, I set my pack down against the picnic table and stood still, staring off into the abyss.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The morning before I was supposed to meet my shuttle driver, I haphazardly threw my pack together. You may come to find out that I’m a professional procrastinator. It’s a tough job, but someone must do it. I planned to have a relaxing day before I set foot on my shakedown hike to double-check my gear. Instead, I threw everything in my pack and drove to Table Rock State Park a couple hours away with no blueprint for the night.

Sources indicate that upon arrival at the state park, I registered as a hiker and asked for a primitive campsite with no preference on location. I would’ve picked the site closest to my car, so I left my fate in her hands. She asked about my campsite location preference, to which I replied, “Anywhere you feel is best, I don’t have a preference.” Oh, but I did! Little did the woman behind the desk know that I had never camped alone, and I was terrified to be alone in the woods at night. She sent me to one of the furthest campsites and wished me luck on the trail.

With only a 5-minute walk to camp, I set my pack down against the picnic table and stood still, staring off into the abyss. Birds chirping, squirrels bolting through crisp leaves, trees creaking, and my tell-tale heart beating louder, louder, louder in my chest. What have I gotten myself into?! The idea of hiking and camping alone was a great idea until I was really doing it, but it was too late to turn back now. The rangers had already closed and locked the park gates until morning. I was stuck there for the night. Do I sleep in my tent or the car?

I set up my tent for the first time outside of my backyard, snapped a photo, and sent it to my husband. A celebratory moment! I had constructed my paper-thin shelter to protect me from the outside world. In my head, the thin tent was comparable to Fort Knox. Good luck to anything wanting to get through! It’s funny how something so basic can provide such a false sense of security. Too nervous for what lies ahead to eat, I brought my food back to the car and took a few pictures of my surroundings as the sun set, including one of myself with a forced smile to convince myself I had this. Now what?

It has been revealed that I spent the next hour texting my husband about how nervous I was and scared of the make-believe monsters that would come capture me in the middle of the night, but my tent would protect me! I closed my eyes and hoped for morning. Instead, I listened to coyotes singing and a dog barking out in the distance all night. I slept for maybe three hours total. Tomorrow is the major day!

You could say I embrace change and enjoy a challenge! My husband and I lived in Colorado for six years, which is where I found my true love for the outdoors. We eloped on one of Colorado's many fourteeners with our two dogs, and since then, it has been one adventure after another. My husband, a seasoned thru-hiker, has encouraged me to embark on my own thru-hiking journey. After logging hundreds of miles in Colorado's wilderness, I completed the Foothills Trail in November 2026 as a shakedown for my upcoming trails. #67932. Two Inexperienced Teens Rescued After 20 Hours on Grossglockner

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (464 w)

Two Inexperienced Teens Rescued After 20 Hours on Grossglockner

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (464 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Two Germans, aged 15 and 18, spent almost 20 hours on Austria’s highest mountain before being evacuated by helicopter on November 15.
  • In a recent development, initially, police reported that the pair had reached the 3,798m summit and become lost while descending.
  • Their ordeal began around 11pm on Saturday, November 14.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Two Germans, aged 15 and 18, spent almost 20 hours on Austria’s highest mountain before being evacuated by helicopter on November 15.

In a recent development, initially, police reported that the pair had reached the 3,798m summit and become lost while descending. The younger climber disputes this, saying they turned back near an alpine hut at 3,454m because his companion felt ill.

Their ordeal began around 11pm on Saturday, November 14. The pair had no previous experience with such a serious mountain but had prepared by reading websites, watching videos, training physically, and asking others for tips. They did carry crampons, an ice axe, a helmet, a rope, a belay device, and extra clothing.

According to recent reports, it took them a long time before they decided to turn around. The descent went well at first, but one spot seemed too dangerous to them. To get around it, they followed someone else’s tracks in the snow, but these suddenly disappeared. While looking for a way, they got stuck in deep snow. The older boy called for help at around 6:30pm on November 15, according to Austria’s public broadcaster, ORF.at.

At first, rescuers tried to guide the pair down by phone. More than two hours later, the boys were still stuck, so a helicopter was dispatched. The rescuers found the pair, exhausted, disoriented, and hypothermic, at around 2,800m.

A rescue helicopter brings the teens to safety. Photo: Mountain Rescue KALS.

Yesterday, rescue leader Peter Tembler criticized their lack of alpine experience and preparation. He told the German Press Agency that the pair lacked sufficient experience for the terrain and winter conditions. He also criticized their late-night departure.

According to Tembler, a section that normally takes four to five hours took them almost 12. Other climbers reportedly advised them against continuing.

Recent findings suggest that tembler believes an increasing number of inexperienced people are attempting serious alpine routes, sometimes encouraged by social media accounts that downplay the difficulty. The disagreement has become a public debate about risk-taking, responsibility, and rescue operations.

Sources indicate that as Austria’s highest peak, Grossglockner is a magnet for climbers of all stripes and has more than its share of controversy. In January 2025, a man abandoned his less experienced girlfriend high on the mountain. She froze to death, and an Austrian court later convicted him of manslaughter for leaving her behind. This summer, an altercation occurred on Grossglockner in which a guide insulted a passing climber and nearly pushed him off a cliff. At the same time, veteran alpinists are still setting bold latest routes here.

According to Der Standard, Grossglockner gets 8,000 to 9,000 ascents each year, with an average of two dozen rescues annually. Between 2005 and 2025, 29 climbers have died on the mountain.

Latest Update: Weekend Warm-Up: Hurricane Chase

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (471 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This episode of the storm-chasing TV series Storm Rising is titled “High Plains Insanity.” Produced by National Geographic, it follows Reed Timmer and Mike Theiss as they attempt to navigate and document an increasingly unpredictable storm season.
  • Sources indicate that the storm-chasing segments are filmed like an action movie but, as Timmer makes clear, thrills are not the primary objective.
  • “That’s why we need to be on the ground directly in the path of these tornadoes,” Timmer explains, “to record data that no one else is getting.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This episode of the storm-chasing TV series Storm Rising is titled “High Plains Insanity.” Produced by National Geographic, it follows Reed Timmer and Mike Theiss as they attempt to navigate and document an increasingly unpredictable storm season.

Sources indicate that the storm-chasing segments are filmed like an action movie but, as Timmer makes clear, thrills are not the primary objective. As the climate changes and disrupts weather patterns, tornadoes are no longer limited to traditional seasons and ranges.

“That’s why we need to be on the ground directly in the path of these tornadoes,” Timmer explains, “to record data that no one else is getting.”.

Sources indicate that driving into a potential tornado in Montana. Photo: Screenshot.

It has been revealed that with hurricane and tornado seasons now overlapping, the duo is forced to split up to cover the widest possible area and collect the most data. For the tornadoes, this means deploying a probe into the funnel.

Sources indicate that up north in the High Plains of the U.S. West and Midwest, Timmer and his dog Gizmo narrowly miss storm after storm. Gizmo is better tech giant but is a very poor navigator, while Timmer isn’t much better. He constantly makes wrong turns as he tries to navigate, drive, and prepare equipment. He does take the time to explain the basic weather science behind what he is failing to catch, such as the conditions that created the baseball-sized hail pummeling his windshield.

Industry observers note that timmer and Gizmo drive through the aftermath of a powerful tornado in the Black Hills of North Dakota. Photo: Screenshot.

In Florida, Theiss sleeps in his car to maintain a constant vigil along the coast. Our current scientific abilities, he explains, allow us to track the movement of hurricane systems with decent accuracy. But predicting their strength is much more difficult. Systems can suddenly turn deadly or fizzle out with equally short notice. In this case, the terrible-looking storm comes to nothing. He heads back up north to rejoin Timmer and Gizmo.

Gizmo buffeted by fierce winds. Photo: Screenshot.

Industry observers note that the reunited trio prepares for a final effort, complete with a windshield-replacement sequence. They immediately drive into the gathering storm, passing through a hail core which, of course, destroys the new windshield. The Lord giveth and taketh away, et cetera. Soon they’re racing on a near-empty tank, as the powerful storm threatens to touch down at any moment.

It’s their last chance this season to deploy the probe. When, after a long, tense chase, they actually manage to do it, both erupt into cheers. Gizmo appears unmoved, despite the fact that this ground probe, deployed in a storm of this type, in this area, has never been deployed before and is sure to yield valuable scientific data.

#67901. Old-School Whitetail Wisdom for Deer Hunting When the Weather Finally Turns Cold

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 16m • 📚 Deep Dive (3144 w)

Old-School Whitetail Wisdom for Deer Hunting When the Weather Finally Turns Cold

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3144 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Without doubt, bass fishing and whitetail deer hunting are the two most popular pastimes of sportsmen searching for outdoor adventures.
  • It has been revealed that wise anglers know that bass do not experience discomfort when water temperatures plummet.
  • According to recent reports, whitetails respond to winter’s periodic onslaughts in much the same way by abandoning their usual haunts until the weather either stabilizes or eventually reverses itself.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Without doubt, bass fishing and whitetail deer hunting are the two most popular pastimes of sportsmen searching for outdoor adventures. And as strange as it may sound, bass and deer are really very much alike, at least in the ways they respond to bitter cold weather.

It has been revealed that wise anglers know that bass do not experience discomfort when water temperatures plummet. However, bass do begin exhibiting changed behavior. Generally bass will drift away from the shallows and into deeper water as the thermometer falls because temperatures in the depths remain relatively stable on a day-to-day basis. Here, their metabolisms begin to wind down. The bass, therefore, do not require as much food intake to sustain various bodily functions. Consequently, these two alterations in their lifestyle can make them very tough to catch for all but the most experienced fishermen.

According to recent reports, whitetails respond to winter’s periodic onslaughts in much the same way by abandoning their usual haunts until the weather either stabilizes or eventually reverses itself. Yet few people, aside from biologists, are aware that deer also eat less as extremely cold weather approaches. Chemical changes take place in their bodies, causing their digestive processes to switch to s-l-o-w. This, in turn, allows for the maintenance of various body systems at a greatly reduced rate of food intake.

In a recent development, another crucial point to emphasize about the anatomies of whitetails is that their brains are comparatively small in relation to their overall body sizes. Therefore, the integrated nervous system coursing throughout their bodies is rudimentary at best. As a result, like most wild creatures that do not possess a sophisticated neural apparatus, their pain thresholds are quite high — making them relatively insensitive to bitter cold temperatures. Many hunters are not aware of this because for generations they’ve been led to believe that when the weather goes sour, deer can be expected to do this or that in order “to seek protection from the elements and be more comfortable.”.

Body comfort actually has little to do with their changed behavior patterns. After all, the northern boundary of the whitetail’s native range extends more than 150 miles beyond the United States/Canadian border to approximately 52° latitude. Anyone who has lived thereabouts can tell you that winter temperatures frequently average -20°. The wind-chill factor often makes it seem as cold as -75°. Therefore, it just doesn’t stand to reason that animal species such as whitetails would be native to such hostile climes were they not virtually immune to such weather.

We’ve even seen evidence of this immunity right on our southern-Ohio farm where it is not uncommon to experience at least several days of -20° temperatures each winter.

Behind my barn there is an old tractor trail that wends its way through a 40-acre oak forest. Numerous times, while hauling out firewood, I’ve seen deer bedded on nearby slopes. Often they reveal a thick dusting of fresh-fallen snow covering their backs — the hollow hairs of their coats providing such superb insulation that their body heat is unable to escape. If I approach too closely, the deer will predictably rise to their feet, shake themselves like soaking-wet dogs and cause clouds of snowflakes to fly — then saunter off to other parts with an air of nonchalance at having been rousted from their beds.

If deer are able to adapt to such gelid temperatures so easily, why is it then, that legions of otherwise knowledgeable hardworking hunters so often strike out when the freeze is on?

Say, for example, that you’ve been hunting in balmy temperatures for several days, have had the opportunity to look over a number of animals but haven’t seen anything you’d really be satisfied with. So you’ve decided to hold out a while longer, hoping you’ll eventually stumble onto “Mr. Significant.”.

According to recent reports, suddenly, you wake up one morning to the sound of icy sleet pinging against your bedroom window. Bounding from the rack, you are shocked to discover that the wind is whistling a siren song and that overnight the temperature has dropped 35°.

After sitting on a stand for several hours that morning without seeing a thing, you look and feel like a popsicle. So you begin moving around — sneak hunting — but eventually conclude that the deer have vanished. By day’s end the temperature has fallen another 10°, a light skiff of hoarfrost blankets the ground and your expectations have long since dwindled. You’ve forgotten entirely about taking a nice buck this season and have begun thinking that if you can just manage to fill your doe tag you’ll be very very lucky.

In a recent development, the scenario is the bane of all hunters living north of the Mason-Dixon Line. Because it’s obvious that the deer couldn’t possibly have just disappeared from the face of the earth, the best prospect for success undoubtedly lies in learning more about their behavioral reactions to severe weather.

Sources indicate that one of the most telling clues to unraveling the mystery of their disappearance can be traced to changes in the whitetails’ body chemistry — the changes that cause them to require less food. Biologists say that this is an annual occurrence and that, like the rut, it is triggered by progressively shorter days and diminished periods of sunlight. Sometime around mid-November, the growth hormone thyroxin, which for the past eight months has been flooding the body, begins dissipating and will remain at a very low level until the following spring.

This shoots down another popular myth about bucks not feeding much during the rut because they are so love struck. Actually, their reduced food intake can be attributed to a conservation measure on the part of nature. In other words, with each additional week of cold weather, food becomes less and less available so nature accordingly reduces the animals’ need for food by enacting significant changes in their body metabolisms.

Hunters should realize that, as the season progresses and as increasing numbers of severe polar blasts begin descending upon their regions, deer can be expected to move around less and less in search of food. The movements they do exhibit are no longer going to be concentrated during the traditional early and late hours of the day but during midday when it is likely to be warmer. Again, the deer are not seeking “comfort” but rather are conserving energy to more efficiently make use of the sharply reduced food supplies.

Recent findings suggest that I’ve seen this happen with such consistency that I now almost consider it axiomatic. At our northern-Minnesota hunting camp, for example, members of our regular group begin bowhunting in October. We’ve learned from more than 80 years of combined experience that the odds of taking a whitetail early in the season are in our favor if we take up early-morning stands, nap during midday when deer are bedded, then resume our vigils late in the afternoon.

Of course the most serious hunters — diehard veterans who are never willing to give up — may find such tactics repugnant.

Industry observers note that yet during the final days of the gun season in December, those in our party who still have not scored have entirely reversed their strategies. Now the order of the day, paradoxically perhaps, is to sleep late in the morning, wait on stand during midday, then quit early. There’s just not enough likelihood of seeing anything move — particularly at dawn’s first light — to justify the oftentimes agonizing ordeal of sitting as still as a statue in weather so bitter cold that it gnaws at your innermost fiber.

According to recent reports, of course the most serious hunters — diehard veterans who are never willing to give up — may find such tactics repugnant. As far as they’re concerned, they want to be in the field every available minute. That’s fine and dandy but, if they want to maximize their chances for success, they should still be willing to make certain adjustments in the way they hunt.

Late in the season, and particularly when the freeze is on, they should stillhunt or sneak hunt early and late in the day when deer are most likely to be sequestered in their beds. During midday, hunters should play the waiting game on stand when deer are inclined to be traveling to and from feeding sites.

But where, exactly, do the deer go when the bottom falls out of the thermometer and ice storms or sheets of wind-driven sleet are lashing the countryside? The three-pronged answer to this is thick cover on a protected south-facing slope in a low-elevation area of terrain.

Two of the most desirable types of thick cover are dense stands of head-high honeysuckle and nearly impenetrable pine plantations. The pines are most often thickets of immature trees that have their whorls of branches close to the ground.

In the face of adverse weather, deer retreat deep into such seclusions where they can wait out the ensuing tempest. Again, trying to stay warm or achieve some other comfort level has little to do with their evasive behavior. Windy stormy weather makes whitetails extremely restless and nervous. By their very nature, whitetails are already hypertensive and are extremely paranoid creatures. When they’re no longer able to detect, classify and catalog sounds and scents because of the competition from noisy winds and erratic air currents, they waste no time finding a place where they can maintain a low profile. Therefore, rather than allowing themselves to remain vulnerable by bedding on their customary hillside benches and ridgelines, they retreat into deep thick cover. This not only helps to block the wind but perhaps also gives them the feeling that hiding from ready view somewhat compensates for their impaired senses.

Once, for a period of several days in the dead of winter, I had the opportunity to watch an eight-point whitetail buck in a fenced enclosure. This was a wild deer that had recently been captured by biologists for use in various nutrition studies. Its temporary fenced-in home was five acres of relatively open hardwood forest with scattered swatches of second-growth ground cover here and there.

In a recent development, whenever the weather was warm, sunny and there was no wind, the buck had a particular place it liked to bed. The deer could see in every direction from the high hammock. Yet whenever a frontal storm system moved through the region and the wind began howling, the deer quickly vacated its usual turf. It always went downhill into a little pocket of thick multiflora rose — the only significant cover in the compound — and buried itself right in the middle.

According to recent reports, one day as snow clouds scudded against an ominously gray sky and ice-riddled branches creaked in the wind, I watched in amazement as the buck laid on his belly for long hours, his front legs outstretched and his chin resting on the ground. Yet when the wind occasionally intensified with its typical freight-train drone, or an ice-laden branch suddenly crashed to the ground, the buck’s head would instantly come up, swiveling in all directions. Assured that nothing was on the prowl, the buck would then rapidly duck back down again. Moments later his head would be up, down, then back up again. Just observing all that nervous energy and pent-up anxiety exhausted me — under these conditions the buck’s entire personality was like a violin string about to snap.

I’m confident that the penned buck would have liked to have had access to much thicker deeper cover to increase his feeling of security. I’m also certain that unconfined deer in their native habitat behave much the same way when the freeze is on. Moreover, a biologist at the research station told me that during one terrible winter storm, the penned buck stayed put for four consecutive days until the weather finally abated.

Recent findings suggest that in addition to tangled jungles of honeysuckle and conifer forests, whitetails also like to retreat into swamps when the freeze is on. Because of the continually decaying organic matter, swamps are always warmer than other regions and this, coupled with the fact that they’re always found in low-lying terrain, keeps them somewhat sheltered from the brunt of the weather.

However, without meaning to again kick the proverbial dead horse, deer don’t seek out swamps in order to stay warm. They go there because past experience has taught them that they’re not likely to bump into hunters in such forbidding territory and, similarly, a swamp is one place where they can continue to effectively rely upon their senses to forewarn them of impending danger.

Yet no matter what type of cover deer may elect to use for hiding, hunting them when the freeze is on can be extremely difficult because the animals’ minds and senses are so preoccupied with monitoring their immediate surroundings. But there are several tactics that seem to be far more productive than others.

First, of course, pay attention to weather forecasts. Deer seem to have built-in barometers that give them advance notice when hostile weather is about to assault their regions. They take due advantage of this insight by stocking up on groceries, instinctively knowing that once the bitter weather strikes it will preclude safe traveling to and from feeding sites for several days. Then, immediately after the frontal system has passed and calmness again prevails, the deer come out of hiding and return to their favorite food plots. Consequently, stand hunting or sneak hunting — just before and immediately after a storm — are two key strategies no enterprising whitetail hunter can afford to pass up.

Cornfields can be prime places to try because, throughout the Midwest and the northern border states, it is becoming an increasingly popular agricultural practice to leave corn standing as long as possible. In the past, it was either chopped or combined sometime in October or November. But with storage costs escalating like never before and future market prices uncertain, many farmers nowadays are leaving the corn in the field until such time as they have a specific need for it or until the price increases. Quite often this means as late as February.

Recent findings suggest that already-picked cornfields are also good bets because a substantial amount of harvest residue may continue to draw deer months after the corn has been combined. On our own cornfields we’re sometimes amazed to see a dozen deer at a time pawing through a foot of snow cover to find spillage.

Sources indicate that I emphasize the importance of finding corn when the freeze is on because native wild foods are becoming more and more sparse with each additional week of winter weather. Other popular agricultural foods such as soybeans are rarely allowed to remain in the field beyond their peak harvest times, so corn is a deer magnet beyond compare.

Industry observers note that hunting during a storm can also pay off. The best opportunity occurs when the temperature does not fall dramatically. This usually means that the wind velocity will not be too fierce and any precipitation is likely to be in the form of huge wet snowflakes that begin clinging to cover like giant globs of cotton candy. Under such conditions, whitetails don’t seem to become as jittery and frantic about their safety and may continue to feed during midday periods. The fluffy snow itself may also pacify them just enough during nonfeeding periods so that they will remain tied to their usual haunts rather than diving headlong into thick security cover.

Any deer hiding within a thicket will merely vamoose out the other side, giving you only a fleeting glimpse of their white semaphore flags signaling goodbye. Instead, try to mentally dope out the lay of the land and then approach from high ground.

According to recent reports, conversely, hunting during the most ravaging freeze-outs offers the least chance of success. Now, patiently waiting on stand is inherently a futile endeavor. The animals simply will not come to you. It is necessary for you to go find them by prowling through swamps, honeysuckle or evergreens.

In a recent development, never try to approach such cover on level ground. Any deer hiding within a thicket will merely vamoose out the other side, giving you only a fleeting glimpse of their white semaphore flags signaling goodbye. Instead, try to mentally dope out the lay of the land and then approach from high ground. This will allow you to look down and through the cover and will make it far easier to spot bedded or sneaking deer.

It has been revealed that another option is to round up several pals and begin staging drives, particularly in the case of expansive pine plantations. Here is a unique situation, not unlike hunting rabbits, where the drivers themselves are likely to be awarded as many shots as the hunters placed on stand. The reason, as we briefly touched on earlier, is because deer that have retreated into the catacombs of thick cover are extremely reluctant to expose themselves, to travel great distances or to sever their close ties with that chosen cover where they’ve decided to holeup. As a result, a buck pushed out by a driver may chart a bounding weaving escape flight that actually takes him only a very short distance before he quickly ducks back down to resume hiding.

Read Next: Tips for Patterning and Hunting a Late-Season Buck.

Because the drivers are likely to see a good deal of shooting, those hunters placed on stand should use portable tree stands situated as high as practical so they are not in the direct line of fire of their approaching partners. Also — and this cannot be emphasized too strongly — every hunter participating in such a maneuver should be fully clad in fluorescent orange clothing and should maintain loud voice contact so everyone is well aware of each other’s location.

According to recent reports, when hunting during freezing stormy weather, wise garment selection also requires careful thought. For sneak hunting or stillhunting, wool is always the best bet because it is noiseless when the fabric grates against brambles and brush. But when toughing out long hours on stand, I rely exclusively upon down-filled duds and bundle up like a snowman.

Recent findings suggest that I’d be the last to say that hunting deer when the freeze is on is purely enjoyable. Human beings just weren’t designed with bitter-cold weather in mind. But when such conditions prevail, any hunter can indeed fill his tag. Just keep in mind the changed behavior the animals are certain to begin exhibiting and plan your strategy accordingly.

This story was originally published in the November 1987 concern of Outdoor Life.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • I’ve been hunting whitetail deer for about 20 years now, and I can still remember what hunting a low deer density, heavy hunting pressure area was like.
  • It wasn’t until about 10 years ago that I started noticing a change.
  • The population has soared across the vast majority of the whitetail’s range, making it easier and easier for us remaining hunters to fill our tags.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I’ve been hunting whitetail deer for about 20 years now, and I can still remember what hunting a low deer density, heavy hunting pressure area was like. When I was a kid, more than 1 million hunters would enter the woods and hunt Pennsylvania’s opening day of rifle season. In my heavily populated area, I always saw a lot more hunters than I did deer.

It wasn’t until about 10 years ago that I started noticing a change. The deer population was skyrocketing and it hasn’t slowed down. Paired with a decline in the hunting population, I’ve experienced the highest deer numbers of my life recently.

But it’s not just in my area. The population has soared across the vast majority of the whitetail’s range, making it easier and easier for us remaining hunters to fill our tags. Tack on the crazy advancements in technology like cellular trail cameras, the latest crossbows, and even technologically-advanced compound bows, and I truly believe deer hunting has never been easier than right now. Here’s why that’s a good thing — sort of.

According to recent reports, across the whitetail’s range, populations are at an all time high. That’s not just my opinion — it’s fact.

Recent findings suggest that “There are between 30 to 35 million whitetails in the U.S. right now,” indicates Kip Adams, chief conservation officer for the National Deer Association. “That’s a crazy number of deer on the landscape. And, the harvest data is backing that up. Nationally, we’ve only surpassed three million bucks harvested annually four times in the last century, all of which occurred within the last five years. We also have the best age structure in the last 100 years. So we’re killing more bucks, and older bucks than ever before.”.

The good news here is that the increasing population has been met with increases in opportunity from the tag allocation side, and the harvest data proves those opportunities are working.

According to recent reports, “We have expanded seasons across the board, higher bag limits than any point in the last century, and more advanced weapons to fill those tags,” indicates Adams. “If you can’t shoot a deer today, you just really aren’t trying very hard.”.

Now, before you go grabbing your pitchforks because you’re still sitting on a pile of tags this season, it’s worth mentioning that Adams and I both agreed that it’s never been easier to kill any deer, but we’re certainly not implying it’s easy to kill a specific deer.

It’s also worth noting that certain areas across the whitetail’s range have seen a decrease in opportunities as diseases like CWD and EHD have impacted herd numbers, and habitat loss continues with urban expansion. But, for most of the whitetail’s range, opportunities abound.

According to recent reports, I’ll be the first to admit I love my cell cameras. I check them almost too often this time of year, but that immediate satisfaction and data grab is addicting. And, that data has helped me dial in the movement patterns of the deer herd in my area based on weather conditions in ways that standard SD card cameras couldn’t. That information, when applied correctly, makes filling a tag substantially easier than just guessing and trying to get lucky.

Take the buck my father tagged last year for example. We had gotten a few photos of him in velvet, keying us in on the area he was using. After planning to stay out of the area and wait for mid to late October when the buck started hitting scrapes, we sat back and waited. Around Oct. 21, we got our first photo of him in the area. And he stayed consistent for three days, hitting the scrape every evening in daylight. On the fourth night, we went in, set up, and a shot opportunity presented itself.

Sure, the stars had to align and the conditions had to be just right for that pattern to exist, but without the technological advancements to trail cameras, I don’t know if we would have gotten a chance at that buck.

Industry observers note that tack on the advancements in our gear. From compounds to crossbows, inlines to straight-walls, and even modern cartridge design, we’ve never been better equipped to shoot deer with more accuracy and efficacy.

“Almost all states in the whitetail’s range allow crossbows for everyone now,” Adams indicates. “Plus, more and more states that used to be shotgun only are now allowing straight-wall cartridges or inline muzzleloaders. All of those additions make it easier for hunters to fill their tags.”.

While the pros speak for themselves, the cons come down to more of an opinion than anything rooted in fact. I have to wonder what all this ease is doing to the heritage of hunting. Hunting was never about being easy, in fact, I’d argue the opposite. It was about the thrill of the chase, the reward of filling your tag after a long season, putting your woodsmanship to the test and coming out on top, and the conservation of one of America’s most valuable resources.

I grew to love hunting because it was challenging. I was unsuccessful a lot, which put a fire in my belly to learn more, hunt harder, and find a way to be successful through the lessons I learned along the way. I wonder if kids like me are getting the same experience, and what the hook for them might be if not.

There’s also the ethical dilemma that an easier hunting experience brings. From the ethics and fair-chase argument relating to cellular trail cameras, to the liberal weapon usage and even baiting tactics in certain states, I fear we’re very close to crossing the line into an unfair advantage over our quarry, if we haven’t gotten there already.

Read Next: Counter Drone Technology Has Come to Deer Hunting and Landowners Are Starting to Fight Back.

In a recent development, it’s up to us as the hunters, and up to the states to decide how much is too much of a good thing. And as the deer populations continue to expand, I personally don’t see a world where the states are the ones that are going to draw the line. So, this season, as you continue to chase that significant buck or a nice doe for the freezer, ask yourself where you proposal to draw the line. And, feel free to join me in wondering how it’s still possible to struggle to fill a tag from time to time.
